title: Arsenic, cadmium and lead in sclerotia of Wolfiporia extensa of Yunnan, China
text:
Arsenic, cadmium and lead in sclerotia of *Wolfiporia extensa* of Yunnan, China

Abstract

*Wolfiporia extensa* (Peck) Ginns, known as “Fuling” in traditional Chinese medicine, is extensively cultivated and consumed in Yunnan Province. Because environmental contamination may result in the accumulation of toxic elements in medicinal fungi, this study investigated the concentrations of arsenic (As), cadmium (Cd), and lead (Pb) in sclerotia collected from the main production areas of Yunnan. Thirty dried samples were microwave-digested and analyzed by inductively coupled plasma–mass spectrometry (ICP-MS). The mean levels (mg kg⁻¹, dry weight) were 0.34 for As, 0.18 for Cd, and 1.25 for Pb. Cadmium in 13.3% of the samples and Pb in 10.0% exceeded the national pharmacopeial limits, whereas all As values remained within the safety threshold. Significant inter-regional variation was observed (p < 0.05), indicating that local geology and anthropogenic activities influence heavy-metal bioaccumulation. Our findings suggest that routine monitoring of cultivation substrates and ambient soil is warranted to ensure the safety of *W. extensa* products.

Keywords: *Wolfiporia extensa*; Heavy metals; Arsenic; Cadmium; Lead; Yunnan; ICP-MS

1. Introduction

*Wolfiporia extensa* is a wood-decay basidiomycete whose sclerotium has been used in East Asian medicine for more than two millennia. In China, Yunnan Province is one of the principal geographic origins of commercial Fuling, thanks to its favorable subtropical climate and extensive pine forests that provide suitable host substrates. Concurrently, Yunnan’s rapid industrial and agricultural development has increased the risk of soil contamination by potentially toxic elements. Arsenic, cadmium, and lead are of particular concern because of their pronounced nephrotoxic, neurotoxic, and carcinogenic potential, and their tendency to accumulate in fungal tissues. Although several studies have documented heavy-metal contents in cultivated macrofungi, systematic surveillance focusing specifically on *W. extensa* sclerotia from Yunnan remains limited. The present study was therefore undertaken to quantify As, Cd, and Pb concentrations in market-bound sclerotia, compare the results among five major production counties, and evaluate the samples against prevailing pharmacopeial safety standards.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Sample collection and preparation

Thirty mature sclerotia of *W. extensa* were obtained from five representative cultivation bases in Yunnan (Lijiang, Chuxiong, Pu’er, Dali, and Baoshan; n = 6 per site) during the 2022–2023 harvest season. Specimens were brushed free of adhering soil, sliced, and dried at 60 °C to constant weight. The dried material was ground to pass through a 0.25-mm mesh sieve and stored in acid-washed polyethylene bags until analysis.

2.2. Chemical analysis

Approximately 0.3 g of each powdered sample was digested in a microwave system (Mars 6, CEM Corporation, USA) using 7 mL of concentrated HNO₃ (65%, Suprapur) and 2 mL of H₂O₂ (30%). Digests were diluted to 50 mL with ultrapure water (18.2 MΩ cm). Arsenic, cadmium, and lead were determined by ICP-MS (Agilent 7900, USA) equipped with a collision/reaction cell to eliminate polyatomic interferences. Multi-element internal standards (Ge, Rh, and Re) were added online for matrix correction. Quality assurance included procedural blanks, duplicate samples (10% of batch), and certified reference material (GBW 10014, cabbage). Mean spike recoveries ranged from 92% to 106%, and relative standard deviations were below 6%.

2.3. Statistical analysis

Data were processed with SPSS 26.0. One-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s test was used to assess regional differences. Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated to examine inter-element relationships. Significance was set at p < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

The descriptive statistics for the three target elements are summarized in Table 1. Across all 30 samples, As concentrations ranged from 0.12 to 0.89 mg kg⁻¹ (mean ± SD: 0.34 ± 0.18 mg kg⁻¹), Cd from 0.05 to 0.42 mg kg⁻¹ (0.18 ± 0.11 mg kg⁻¹), and Pb from 0.45 to 3.12 mg kg⁻¹ (1.25 ± 0.72 mg kg⁻¹). According to the Chinese Pharmacopoeia (2020 edition) general limit for As (≤ 2.0 mg kg⁻¹), Cd (≤ 0.3 mg kg⁻¹), and Pb (≤ 5.0 mg kg⁻¹) in medicinal plants and fungi, none of the samples exceeded the As threshold, whereas four samples (13.3%) surpassed the Cd limit and three (10.0%) exceeded the Pb limit.

Regional ANOVA revealed statistically significant differences for Cd and Pb (p < 0.05). Sclerotia from Pu’er exhibited the highest mean Cd level (0.29 ± 0.08 mg kg⁻¹), whereas those from Baoshan recorded the greatest Pb concentration (1.98 ± 0.85 mg kg⁻¹). Lijiang samples consistently showed the lowest levels of all three metals. Pearson correlation analysis indicated a moderately positive correlation between Pb and Cd (r = 0.62, p < 0.01), while As was only weakly associated with the other two elements (r < 0.30, p > 0.05).

4. Discussion

The overall heavy-metal burdens observed in Yunnan *W. extensa* were comparable to or lower than those reported for wild-growing mushrooms from polluted areas of central China and eastern Europe, yet slightly higher than values previously noted for greenhouse-cultivated sclerotia in Fujian Province. The conspicuous inter-regional variation implies that local edaphic and environmental factors strongly modulate element uptake. For instance, the elevated Cd and Pb in Pu’er and Baoshan may reflect natural geochemical anomalies in western Yunnan as well as legacy contamination from adjacent lead–zinc mining operations. The significant Pb–Cd correlation further suggests common anthropogenic sources, possibly including atmospheric deposition from fossil-fuel combustion and phosphate fertilizer application in nearby agricultural zones.

From a toxicological perspective, the majority of the present samples met the pharmacopeial criteria, indicating that Yunnan Fuling is generally safe for decoction and extract preparation. Nevertheless, the detection of Cd and Pb above statutory limits in roughly 10–13% of the batch underscores the necessity of pre-harvest risk screening. Unlike leafy vegetables, fungal sclerotia are consumed in relatively small daily doses; however, chronic low-level exposure to Cd and Pb remains a public-health concern because of their long biological half-lives. A limitation of this study is the absence of paired topsoil and substrate analyses, which precludes definitive source apportionment. Future work should integrate rhizosphere soil chemistry, airborne particulate monitoring, and speciation analysis to distinguish bioavailable fractions.

5. Conclusion

This survey demonstrates that arsenic, cadmium, and lead are detectable in *Wolfiporia extensa* sclerotia from Yunnan, but only cadmium and lead occasionally exceed national pharmacopeial limits. Marked geographic variation points to site-specific contamination drivers rather than province-wide pollution. To safeguard the quality of this economically and medicinally important fungus, continuous heavy-metal monitoring, cultivation-site selection, and substrate pre-treatment should be implemented as integral components of good agricultural practice in Yunnan’s *W. extensa* industry.

title: In-season root-zone N management for mitigating greenhouse gas emission and reactive N losses in intensive wheat production
text:
In-season root-zone N management for mitigating greenhouse gas emission and reactive N losses in intensive wheat production

Abstract

Intensive wheat systems rely on heavy nitrogen (N) fertilization, causing substantial nitrous oxide (N₂O) emissions and reactive nitrogen (Nr) losses. A two-year field study was conducted to evaluate in-season root-zone N management (RNM) against conventional broadcasting (CB) and standard farmer practice (FP) in the North China Plain. The RNM strategy combined soil nitrate testing and canopy NDVI sensors to guide split side-dress applications banded directly within the root zone. We measured N₂O flux, ammonia (NH₃) volatilization, nitrate (NO₃⁻) leaching, grain yield, and nitrogen use efficiency (NUE). Compared with FP, RNM reduced cumulative N₂O by 28–34%, NH₃ by 22–27%, and NO₃⁻ leaching by 31–36% without compromising grain yield. NUE increased from approximately 39% under FP to 49% under RNM, despite a 25% reduction in total N input. These results demonstrate that synchronizing N supply with crop demand via in-season root-zone management is a promising strategy to mitigate the environmental footprint of intensive wheat production.

Keywords: Nitrogen use efficiency; Nitrous oxide; Ammonia volatilization; Nitrate leaching; Precision fertilization; *Triticum aestivum*

Introduction

Global intensive wheat (*Triticum aestivum* L.) production underpins food security yet remains heavily dependent on synthetic N inputs. In many high-yielding regions, blanket broadcasting of urea chronically exceeds actual crop demand, generating significant environmental externalities including N₂O emissions, NH₃ volatilization, and NO₃⁻ leaching. These reactive N losses not only waste fossil fuel energy embedded in fertilizer but also contribute to greenhouse gas forcing, atmospheric PM₂.₅ formation, and eutrophication of aquatic ecosystems.

Conventional split applications improve upon single basal doses yet still rely on fixed empirical schedules rather than real-time crop needs. In-season root-zone N management (RNM)—an approach integrating soil mineral N testing with proximal canopy sensing to guide banded side-dressing—offers the potential to synchronize N availability with root uptake dynamics. By localizing nutrients directly within the rhizosphere and adjusting rates according to growth stage, RNM could reduce N surpluses in the soil profile. However, simultaneous field quantification of greenhouse gas and Nr losses under RNM in winter wheat remains limited. We hypothesized that RNM would significantly decrease N₂O, NH₃, and NO₃⁻ losses compared with both single basal broadcasting and standard farmer split practices, while maintaining grain yield. This study was designed to test that hypothesis across two consecutive growing seasons in a representative intensive wheat system.

Materials and Methods

A two-year (2021–2023) field experiment was conducted on a silt-loam soil (Typic Hapludalf, pH 7.2, organic C 14.2 g kg⁻¹, bulk density 1.35 Mg m⁻³) at the Luancheng Agro-Ecosystem Station (37.9° N, 114.7° E). Winter wheat (cv. Jimai 22) was sown at 2.25 × 10⁶ plants ha⁻¹ in mid-October and harvested in early June. Three N treatments were arranged in a randomized complete block design with four replicates (plot size 45 m²): (1) Farmer Practice (FP): 240 kg N ha⁻¹ as urea, split 50% basal and 50% at jointing, broadcast by hand; (2) Conventional Broadcasting (CB): 210 kg N ha⁻¹ applied once as basal broadcast; (3) Root-zone N Management (RNM): 180 kg N ha⁻¹ total, with 30% basal incorporation, and 70% side-dressed in two splits at tillering (Zadoks GS 25) and flag-leaf (GS 37) stages based on soil NO₃⁻–N (0–30 cm) thresholds (<20 mg kg⁻¹) and GreenSeeker™ NDVI-guided variable rates. All plots received 120 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹ and 90 kg K₂O ha⁻¹ basally.

Static closed chambers (20 cm diameter, 25 cm height) measured N₂O flux twice weekly and for five days following fertilization or >10 mm rainfall. Gas samples were analyzed by electron-capture gas chromatography. NH₃ volatilization was captured using continuous airflow enclosures (0.4 m² base) with boric acid traps; airflow was maintained at 15–20 L min⁻¹. Ceramic cup suction lysimeters installed at 60 cm depth collected soil solution biweekly for NO₃⁻–N determination via continuous flow analysis. Grain yield was measured at physiological maturity from a 10 m² harvest area and adjusted to 12.5% moisture. NUE was calculated as (grain N uptake / N applied) × 100%. Data were subjected to two-way ANOVA (year × treatment) using SAS v9.4, with means separated by Tukey’s HSD at *P* < 0.05.

Results

RNM significantly mitigated reactive N losses across both years. Cumulative seasonal N₂O emissions were 1.42 and 1.38 kg N ha⁻¹ under FP in 2021–2022 and 2022–2023, respectively; CB produced the highest emissions (1.68 and 1.61 kg N ha⁻¹). RNM reduced these to 1.01 and 0.98 kg N ha⁻¹ (*P* < 0.05), corresponding to 28.9% and 34.1% reductions versus FP. NH₃ volatilization followed a similar pattern: FP lost 18.2 and 17.9 kg N ha⁻¹ seasonally, whereas CB lost 24.5 and 23.8 kg N ha⁻¹. RNM lowered NH₃ losses to 13.8 and 13.4 kg N ha⁻¹, representing 24.2% and 25.1% reductions relative to FP, and 43.7% relative to CB.

NO₃⁻ leaching losses at 60 cm depth were markedly reduced under RNM. Two-year averages were 14.7 and 16.1 kg N ha⁻¹ for FP, 15.3 and 17.5 kg N ha⁻¹ for CB, but only 9.4 and 11.2 kg N ha⁻¹ for RNM (31–36% lower than FP). Despite lower N inputs, grain yield did not differ significantly among treatments (*P* = 0.18). Mean yields were 8.92, 8.85, and 9.04 t ha⁻¹ for FP, CB, and RNM, respectively. Accordingly, NUE was substantially improved under RNM, reaching 48.2% and 49.6% compared with 38.4% and 39.1% for FP, and 31.2% and 32.5% for CB. These data indicate that reducing total N by 25% through precision root-zone delivery did not constrain productivity.

Discussion

Our findings demonstrate that in-season root-zone N management can effectively decouple high wheat productivity from high reactive N losses. The marked decline in N₂O emissions under RNM likely reflects reduced temporal asynchrony between soil mineral N and crop uptake. By withholding a majority of N until tillering and flag-leaf stages, and banding it directly adjacent to active roots, RNM minimized substrate accumulation in the topsoil during wet periods that otherwise fuel denitrification. The steep NH₃ reductions observed are attributable to both lower total N rates and the avoidance of surface-broadcast urea; banding below the surface reduced contact with urease-rich residues and decreased wind-driven volatilization.

Interestingly, CB generated the greatest N₂O and NH₃ losses, underscoring that a single heavy basal application overwhelms early-season demand and creates “hot moments” of loss. The lack of yield penalty under RNM—despite a 60 kg N ha⁻¹ reduction relative to FP—suggests that conventional farmer rates in this region contain a sizable insurance surplus that is poorly utilized when broadcast. The NUE of ~49% achieved here is among the highest reported for intensive winter wheat and aligns with precision agriculture studies employing sensor-guided variable-rate N.

Reduced NO₃⁻ leaching is particularly meaningful for the North China Plain, where shallow groundwater NO₃⁻ contamination frequently exceeds WHO limits. A caveat is that these results derive from a single cultivar and soil type; sandy or poorly structured soils may alter leaching dynamics. Nonetheless, the consistency of benefits across two climatically distinct years indicates robustness. Adoption barriers remain logistical, as RNM requires soil testing and side-dress equipment, but the environmental and efficiency gains justify wider deployment.

Conclusion

In-season root-zone N management reduced seasonal N₂O emissions by up to 34%, NH₃ volatilization by 25%, and NO₃⁻ leaching by 36% relative to standard farmer practice, while maintaining grain yield and increasing NUE to nearly 50%. These results support a transition from broadcast fertilization to precision, root-zone delivery systems in intensive wheat production. Such synchronization of N supply with crop demand offers a scalable pathway to mitigate greenhouse gas and reactive N footprints without compromising food security. Future research should address economic optimization, long-term soil carbon interactions, and scalability across diverse soil–climate gradients to facilitate farmer adoption.

title: Morphology, Phylogeny, and Pathogenicity of Pestalotioid Species on Camellia oleifera in China
text: Camellia oleifera is an economically important oil-bearing tree species in China; however, diseases associated with pestalotioid fungi significantly threaten sustainable production. To clarify the species diversity, phylogenetic relationships, and pathogenicity of these pathogens, a systematic survey was conducted across major *C. oleifera* cultivation regions. Pestalotioid fungi were isolated from symptomatic leaves, fruits, and twigs displaying anthracnose-like lesions or shoot dieback, and identified using an integrative taxonomic approach combining cultural characteristics, conidial morphology, and multilocus phylogenetic analyses based on internal transcribed spacer (ITS), translation elongation factor 1-alpha (*tef1*), and β-tubulin (*tub2*) sequences. Pathogenicity was assessed through wound-inoculation assays on detached leaves and potted seedlings, fulfilling Koch’s postulates. Several pestalotioid species, including members of *Pestalotiopsis* and allied genera, were identified. Phylogenetic analyses resolved distinct, well-supported clades corresponding to morphological groups and indicated the presence of cryptic or undescribed taxa. Although all tested isolates caused typical symptoms on *C. oleifera*, significant variation in virulence was observed among species and geographical origins, suggesting pathogen population heterogeneity. These results provide the first comprehensive characterization of pestalotioid pathogens on *C. oleifera* in China, elucidate their taxonomic status and evolutionary relationships, and underscore their roles as important causal agents, thereby informing integrated disease management strategies for oil-tea plantations.

title: Identification and Detection of Botryosphaeria dothidea from Kiwifruit (Actinidia chinensis) in China
text:
Identification and Detection of *Botryosphaeria dothidea* from Kiwifruit (*Actinidia chinensis*) in China

Abstract

Kiwifruit stem canker caused by *Botryosphaeria dothidea* is a devastating disease affecting *Actinidia chinensis* production in China. Accurate identification and rapid detection are essential for effective disease management. In this study, 86 symptomatic samples were collected from major kiwifruit-growing regions in Shaanxi, Sichuan, and Henan provinces. Fungal pathogens were isolated using tissue segment plating on potato dextrose agar (PDA). Morphological characterization combined with multi-locus phylogenetic analysis of the internal transcribed spacer (ITS) and translation elongation factor 1-alpha (TEF1-α) regions confirmed the identity of *B. dothidea*. Pathogenicity tests fulfilled Koch's postulates. Additionally, a species-specific PCR assay was developed for rapid detection. Results showed that 42 isolates (48.8%) were identified as *B. dothidea*. The specific primer pair BdF/BdR amplified a 428-bp fragment exclusively from *B. dothidea*, with a detection limit of 10 pg. This study provides reliable methods for the identification and early detection of *B. dothidea* in kiwifruit orchards.

Keywords
*Botryosphaeria dothidea*; *Actinidia chinensis*; kiwifruit stem canker; molecular identification; species-specific PCR; phylogenetic analysis

1. Introduction

Kiwifruit (*Actinidia chinensis* Planch.) is an economically important fruit crop native to China, with extensive cultivation in Shaanxi, Sichuan, and Henan provinces. In recent years, stem canker, branch dieback, and fruit rot caused by Botryosphaeriaceae fungi have emerged as serious threats to the kiwifruit industry. Among these pathogens, *Botryosphaeria dothidea* (Moug.: Fr.) Ces. & De Not. is one of the most prevalent and destructive species, causing significant yield losses and tree mortality in commercial orchards.

Traditional identification relying solely on morphological characteristics is often ambiguous due to the high phenotypic plasticity of *B. dothidea* and the presence of cryptic species within the Botryosphaeriaceae. Although cultural and microscopic examinations remain valuable, they are frequently insufficient to distinguish closely related taxa. Molecular techniques, particularly DNA sequencing of conserved loci, have become essential for accurate species delineation. Furthermore, early and specific detection is crucial for implementing timely phytosanitary measures and preventing the spread of contaminated nursery stock. The objectives of this study were to (i) isolate and characterize *B. dothidea* from diseased kiwifruit tissues collected across major production regions in China, (ii) confirm its identity through integrated morphological and phylogenetic analyses, and (iii) develop a rapid, species-specific PCR assay for routine diagnostic use.

2. Materials and Methods

Sample collection and pathogen isolation. Symptomatic kiwifruit branches and fruits showing typical canker, lenticel rot, and exudate symptoms were collected from commercial orchards in Shaanxi (*n* = 35), Sichuan (*n* = 31), and Henan (*n* = 20) provinces during the 2022–2023 growing seasons. Small tissue pieces (5 × 5 mm) from the lesion margins were surface-sterilized in 75% ethanol for 30 s, 2% sodium hypochlorite for 2 min, rinsed three times in sterile distilled water, and plated on potato dextrose agar (PDA) supplemented with 50 mg/L streptomycin. Plates were incubated at 25°C in the dark for 3–7 days. Mycelial tips from emerging colonies were transferred to fresh PDA to obtain pure cultures, which were stored on PDA slants at 4°C.

Morphological characterization. Colony morphology, color, texture, and growth rate were recorded after 7 days on PDA at 25°C. Conidial morphology was examined using a light microscope (Olympus BX53) after inducing sporulation on pine needle agar (PNA). Measurements of 50 conidia per isolate were recorded.

Molecular identification and phylogenetic analysis. Genomic DNA was extracted from 7-day-old cultures using a modified CTAB method. The ITS region and partial TEF1-α gene were amplified using primer pairs ITS1/ITS4 and EF1-728F/EF1-986R, respectively. PCR was performed in a 25 μL reaction volume under the following conditions: initial denaturation at 94°C for 5 min, 35 cycles of 94°C for 30 s, 55°C for 30 s, and 72°C for 1 min, with a final extension at 72°C for 7 min. Amplicons were sequenced bi-directionally. Sequences were edited using BioEdit and subjected to BLASTn analysis against the NCBI GenBank database. A concatenated dataset of ITS and TEF1-α sequences was aligned with reference strains using MAFFT. Maximum likelihood phylogenetic trees were constructed using IQ-TREE with 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates.

Pathogenicity test. A representative isolate (BD-KW1, from Shaanxi) was tested on healthy 2-year-old potted kiwifruit branches (cv. Hayward). Branches were wounded with a sterile scalpel and inoculated with 5-mm mycelial plugs from 7-day-old cultures. Control branches received sterile PDA plugs. Inoculated plants were maintained in a greenhouse at 25 ± 2°C with 85% relative humidity. Lesion lengths were measured at 7 and 14 days post-inoculation (dpi), and the pathogen was re-isolated to fulfill Koch's postulates.

Specific PCR detection. Species-specific primers BdF (5'-GCTCTCGTGGTCGGTCTG-3') and BdR (5'-CGGAGGACGAAAACGACGA-3') were designed based on single nucleotide polymorphisms in the TEF1-α gene alignment. PCR specificity was evaluated against 15 non-target fungal species, including *Macrophomina phaseolina*, *Fusarium solani*, *Colletotrichum gloeosporioides*, *Neofusicoccum parvum*, and *Diplodia seriata*. Sensitivity was determined using 10-fold serial dilutions of *B. dothidea* genomic DNA ranging from 10 ng to 0.01 pg per reaction.

3. Results and Analysis

Pathogen isolation and morphological identification. A total of 142 fungal isolates were recovered from 86 symptomatic samples. *Botryosphaeria dothidea* was identified from 42 isolates, representing a sample incidence of 48.8% (18 from Shaanxi, 15 from Sichuan, and 9 from Henan). Colonies on PDA were initially white and fluffy, becoming olivaceous gray to dark green after 7 days, with dense aerial mycelium and irregular margins. The average radial growth rate was 9.2 ± 0.4 mm/day at 25°C. Conidia were hyaline, unicellular, fusiform to ellipsoidal, measuring 20.5–24.8 × 5.2–6.8 μm (mean: 22.3 × 5.9 μm). Conidiomata produced on PNA were pycnidial, dark, globose to subglobose, and ostiolate.

Molecular and phylogenetic identification. BLASTn analysis of the ITS sequences (520–540 bp) from representative isolates showed 99–100% identity with *B. dothidea* sequences in GenBank (e.g., accessions KY927487, MZ675443). The TEF1-α sequences (280–300 bp) exhibited 99% similarity to the ex-type strain CBS 115476. Phylogenetic analysis based on the concatenated ITS-TEF1-α dataset placed all test isolates in a monophyletic, well-supported clade (ultrafast bootstrap value = 98%) with authenticated *B. dothidea* strains, clearly distinguishing them from closely related species such as *B. ribis*, *Neofusicoccum parvum*, and *Diplodia seriata*.

Pathogenicity assay. All inoculated branches developed dark necrotic lesions at the wound sites within 7 dpi. By 14 dpi, lesion lengths averaged 3.2 ± 0.5 cm on inoculated branches, compared to 0.3 ± 0.1 cm on negative control branches (Student’s *t*-test, *P* < 0.01). Characteristic internal wood discoloration and bark cracking were observed. *Botryosphaeria dothidea* was successfully re-isolated from all symptomatic tissues, confirming Koch's postulates.

Specific PCR detection assay. The primer pair BdF/BdR specifically amplified a single 428-bp fragment from all 42 *B. dothidea* isolates but not from any of the 15 non-target fungal species tested. No cross-reactivity was observed with other common kiwifruit pathogens. The detection limit of the assay was 10 pg of genomic DNA per 25 μL reaction, demonstrating high sensitivity suitable for routine diagnosis.

4. Discussion

This study successfully isolated and identified *B. dothidea* as a prominent pathogen associated with kiwifruit stem canker in major production areas of China. The overall isolation frequency of 48.8% across three provinces underscores its significant epidemiological role in kiwifruit disease complexes. While initial morphological characterization provided a tentative identification, multi-locus phylogenetic analysis proved indispensable for definitive species confirmation, reflecting the well-documented cryptic diversity within the Botryosphaeriaceae. The concatenated ITS-TEF1-α phylogeny robustly differentiated *B. dothidea* from morphologically similar species such as *N. parvum* and *D. seriata*, reinforcing the necessity of integrating molecular data in modern phytopathological diagnostics.

The pathogenicity results unequivocally demonstrated that *B. dothidea* is capable of causing typical canker symptoms on kiwifruit branches, consistent with previous reports from New Zealand, Italy, and Chile. The rapid lesion expansion observed under greenhouse conditions suggests that wound entry followed by latent infection may play important roles in natural epidemics, particularly during pruning and storm

title: Dissipation kinetics, pre-harvest residue limits, and dietary risk assessment of the systemic fungicide metalaxyl in Swiss chard grown under greenhouse conditions
text: Swiss chard (*Beta vulgaris* subsp. *vulgaris*) is a highly nutritious leafy vegetable widely consumed worldwide. Greenhouse cultivation has become increasingly prevalent to ensure year-round production; however, the controlled environment may significantly alter pesticide dissipation patterns compared to open-field conditions, potentially resulting in higher residue levels and prolonged persistence. Metalaxyl, a systemic acylalanine fungicide, is extensively applied to control oomycete diseases in various crops, including leafy vegetables. Due to its systemic properties, metalaxyl can be readily translocated throughout plant tissues, raising concerns regarding residual accumulation in edible portions and subsequent dietary exposure. Although maximum residue limits (MRLs) have been established for metalaxyl in several commodities, specific residue and dissipation data for Swiss chard, particularly under greenhouse conditions, remain scarce. Furthermore, pre-harvest residue limits (PHRLs), which serve as practical guidance for safe harvesting intervals, are frequently unavailable for minor crops such as Swiss chard. To ensure consumer food safety and facilitate compliance with international trade standards, comprehensive studies investigating pesticide dissipation kinetics, establishing scientifically based PHRLs, and conducting dietary risk assessments are urgently needed. This study was therefore conducted to elucidate the dissipation behavior of metalaxyl in Swiss chard grown under greenhouse conditions, propose PHRLs at different pre-harvest intervals, and evaluate the potential dietary risk for Chinese consumers using supervised trial residue data. The findings will provide critical scientific support for the rational application of metalaxyl and the establishment of MRLs for Swiss chard in both domestic and international markets.

title: Toward an adverse outcome pathway for impaired growth: Mitochondrial dysfunction impairs growth in early life stages of the fathead minnow (Pimephales promelas)
text: Exposure to 50 µM rotenone from 0–7 days post-hatch (dph) caused a 42% reduction in basal mitochondrial respiration (*p* < 0.01) and a 35% decrease in whole-body ATP content compared with controls. By 14 dph, treated larvae exhibited 28% lower standard length (9.2 ± 0.4 mm vs. 12.8 ± 0.3 mm; *p* < 0.001) and 31% reduced wet weight (*p* < 0.001). Regression analysis revealed a strong correlation between mitochondrial oxygen consumption rate and larval length (*r*² = 0.78, *p* < 0.001), suggesting that energy limitation directly constrains somatic growth. These results support the proposed adverse outcome pathway linking mitochondrial dysfunction to impaired growth in early life stages of the fathead minnow. Disruption of oxidative phosphorylation appears to be a molecular initiating event that propagates through reduced ATP biosynthesis to a diminished growth phenotype, confirming the utility of mitochondrial endpoints as predictive biomarkers in ecotoxicological risk assessment.

title: Enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers were not effective in reducing N2O emissions from a drip-irrigated cotton field in arid region of Northwestern China
text:
Enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers were not effective in reducing N2O emissions from a drip-irrigated cotton field in arid region of Northwestern China

Abstract

Agricultural soils are a major source of atmospheric nitrous oxide (N₂O). Enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers (EEFs) have been widely promoted as a mitigation strategy; however, their performance in arid, drip-irrigated agroecosystems remains uncertain. A field experiment was conducted during the 2023 growing season in the Aksu Prefecture of Xinjiang, Northwest China, to evaluate the effects of three EEFs—urea with dicyandiamide (DCD), polymer-coated urea (PCU), and stabilized urea (SU)—on N₂O emissions, soil inorganic nitrogen dynamics, and cotton yield in a mulched drip-irrigation system. N₂O fluxes were measured using the static chamber method and analyzed by gas chromatography. Results showed that all treatments produced low background N₂O fluxes punctuated by transient emission peaks following irrigation or rainfall events. Cumulative N₂O emissions were 1.85, 1.72, 1.68, and 1.79 kg N₂O-N ha⁻¹ for conventional urea, urea+DCD, PCU, and SU, respectively. No significant differences were detected among treatments (*P* > 0.05). Corresponding emission factors ranged from 0.56% to 0.62%, with no mitigation benefit from EEFs. Soil ammonium and nitrate concentrations differed marginally in early season but converged by the flowering stage. Seed cotton yields were comparable across treatments, averaging 5,640 kg ha⁻¹. These findings indicate that under the water-limited, alkaline conditions of the study region, EEFs did not effectively reduce N₂O emissions from drip-irrigated cotton fields. Alternative strategies integrating water and nutrient management may be required to achieve meaningful greenhouse gas mitigation in such arid environments.

Keywords: Enhanced efficiency fertilizers; Nitrous oxide; Drip irrigation; Cotton; Arid region; Nitrification inhibitor

1. Introduction

Nitrous oxide (N₂O) is a potent greenhouse gas with a global warming potential approximately 265 times that of carbon dioxide over a 100-year horizon and a principal agent in stratospheric ozone depletion. Agricultural soils contribute roughly 60% of global anthropogenic N₂O emissions, primarily driven by microbial nitrification and denitrification processes that are stimulated by nitrogen (N) fertilization. In China, the expansion of intensified cropping systems has amplified soil N₂O fluxes, prompting urgent needs for mitigation measures.

The Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in Northwest China represents one of the world’s largest contiguous cotton-producing areas, with over 85% of the national output. Cotton cultivation in this region relies almost exclusively on mulched drip irrigation, a water-saving technique that delivers N fertilizer directly to the root zone through fertigation. While drip irrigation improves water and nutrient use efficiency, the pulsed wetting cycles can create localized anaerobic conditions within the soil profile, potentially enhancing N₂O production via denitrification. Concurrently, the overall arid climate—characterized by low precipitation (<100 mm annually), high evapotranspiration, and alkaline soils—may constrain microbial activity and N cycling rates.

Enhanced efficiency fertilizers (EEFs), including nitrification inhibitors, urease inhibitors, and controlled-release formulations, have shown promise in reducing N₂O emissions in humid and semi-humid croplands by slowing N transformation and matching supply with crop demand. However, evidence from hyper-arid, drip-irrigated systems remains scarce and inconsistent. We hypothesized that EEFs would suppress seasonal N₂O emissions compared with conventional urea in a Northwest Chinese cotton system. To test this, we conducted a randomized field trial comparing conventional urea with urea amended with DCD, PCU, and stabilized urea, with the objectives of quantifying growing-season N₂O fluxes, estimating emission factors, and assessing agronomic performance.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Experimental site

The field experiment was carried out at the experimental station of Xinjiang Academy of Agricultural Sciences (40°32′ N, 80°45′ E; elevation 1,032 m) during April–October 2023. The region has a typical continental arid climate. Mean annual air temperature is 11.2 °C, and annual precipitation averages 65 mm. The soil is a sandy loam (Typic Torriorthents) with pH 8.4 (1:2.5 soil:water), soil organic carbon 6.8 g kg⁻¹, total N 0.75 g kg⁻¹, available phosphorus 18.4 mg kg⁻¹, and bulk density 1.45 g cm⁻³ in the 0–20 cm layer.

2.2. Experimental design and field management

The experiment followed a randomized complete block design with four treatments and three replicates. Plot size was 6 m × 8 m (48 m²). The treatments were: (1) conventional urea (Urea); (2) urea with nitrification inhibitor DCD at 5% of N rate (Urea+DCD); (3) polymer-coated urea (PCU, 90-day release); and (4) stabilized urea containing both urease and nitrification inhibitors (SU). All treatments received an identical N rate of 300 kg N ha⁻¹, which represents local conventional practice. Phosphorus (120 kg P₂O₅ ha⁻¹ as triple superphosphate) and potassium (75 kg K₂O ha⁻¹ as potassium sulfate) were applied uniformly as basal fertilizers before sowing. For Urea and Urea+DCD, 40% of the N was applied basally and the remaining 60% was split equally among three fertigation events (early flowering, full flowering, and boll-setting stages). PCU and SU were applied entirely as a single basal dose.

Cotton (*Gossypium hirsutum* L. cv. Xinluzao 72) was sown on 20 April under plastic mulch with a row spacing of 66 cm + 10 cm (narrow-wide configuration) and a plant density of 240,000 plants ha⁻¹. Drip tapes were laid under the mulch with emitters spaced 30 cm apart and a discharge rate of 2.6 L h⁻¹. Irrigation was scheduled based on crop evapotranspiration, totaling 450 mm across 10 events. Weeds, pests, and diseases were controlled following standard local practices.

2.3. N₂O sampling and analysis

N₂O fluxes were measured using the static closed chamber method. Stainless-steel base frames (50 cm × 50 cm) were inserted 10 cm into the soil between cotton rows immediately after sowing and remained in place throughout the season. During sampling, a chamber (50 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm) lined with reflective insulation was placed onto the groove of the base frame. Samples were withdrawn with a 30 mL polypropylene syringe at 0, 15, and 30 min after closure. Sampling frequency was every 3–7 days during the non-irrigated periods and every 1–2 days for one week following each irrigation or rainfall event. Gas samples were analyzed within 24 h using a gas chromatograph (Agilent 7890B) equipped with an electron capture detector (ECD) for N₂O. Fluxes were calculated from the linear increase in gas concentration over time.

Cumulative N₂O emissions were computed by linear interpolation of fluxes between sampling intervals. The emission factor (EF) was calculated as the difference in cumulative N₂O emission between fertilized plots and an unfertilized control (measured in three additional plots), divided by the total N applied, expressed as a percentage. Soil temperature at 10 cm depth and volumetric water content (0–10 cm) were recorded concurrently with gas sampling using a portable TDR probe. Soil inorganic N (NH₄⁺-N and NO₃⁻-N) was extracted with 1 M KCl and determined by continuous flow analyzer (Seal AA3) at weekly intervals.

2.4. Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using SPSS 26.0. Treatment means were compared by the least significant difference (LSD) test at *P* < 0.05. Pearson correlation analysis was performed to examine relationships between N₂O fluxes and environmental variables.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1. N₂O flux dynamics

Seasonal N₂O fluxes were generally low across all treatments, ranging from near-zero to 5.2 mg N₂O-N m⁻² h⁻¹. Background fluxes during dry soil conditions were consistently below 0.3 mg N₂O-N m⁻² h⁻¹. Distinct emission peaks were observed within 24–72 h after each drip irrigation event and after a 12.4 mm rainfall on 15 June. The highest single peak (5.2 mg N₂O-N m⁻² h⁻¹) occurred in the Urea treatment following the first fertigation. EEF treatments exhibited slightly attenuated peaks (4.5–4.8 mg N₂O-N m⁻² h⁻¹), but the differences were not statistically significant. By mid-July, as soil temperature peaked and irrigation frequency increased, all treatments displayed similarly low fluxes, suggesting that substrate availability rather than fertilizer type governed the post-irrigation pulses.

3.2. Cumulative N₂O emissions and emission factors

Growing-season cumulative N₂O emissions were 1.85 ± 0.21, 1.72 ± 0.18, 1.68 ± 0.16, and 1.79 ± 0.19 kg N₂O-N ha⁻¹ for Urea, Urea+DCD, PCU, and SU, respectively (Fig. 1). ANOVA revealed no significant treatment effect (*P* = 0.74). The unfertilized control emitted 0.98 kg N₂O-N ha⁻¹. Consequently, the calculated emission factors were 0.62%, 0.58%, 0.56%, and 0.60% for the four fertilized treatments. The differences in EF among EEFs and urea were marginal and did not reach statistical significance (*P* = 0.68). These values are at the lower bound of the IPCC default EF of 1.0% for direct N₂O emissions from managed soils.

3.3. Soil inorganic nitrogen and environmental drivers

Soil NH₄⁺-N concentrations peaked immediately after basal fertilization and fertigation, declining rapidly within one week. Urea+DCD and SU maintained slightly higher NH₄⁺-N levels during the first two weeks; however, by the squaring stage, concentrations converged across all treatments. NO₃⁻-N dynamics followed an inverse pattern, with no sustained reduction in nitrification apparent in the inhibitor treatments over the season. Soil volumetric water content fluctuated between 8% and 22%, rarely exceeding the threshold required for substantial denitrification. Correlation analysis indicated that N₂O fluxes were positively correlated with soil water content (*r* = 0.62, *P* < 0.01) and soil temperature (*r* = 0.45, *P* < 0.05), but not with soil NO₃⁻ concentration (*r* = 0.21, *P* > 0.05).

3.4. Cotton yield and nitrogen use efficiency

Seed cotton yields were 5,680, 5,720, 5,610, and 5,560 kg ha⁻¹ for Urea, Urea+DCD, PCU, and SU, respectively. Yield differences among treatments were not significant (*P* = 0.83). Similarly, aboveground biomass and lint percentage did not differ significantly. These results indicate that the EEF formulations provided no agronomic advantage over split-applied conventional urea under the experimental conditions.

4. Discussion

Our results demonstrate that EEFs, including nitrification inhibitors and polymer-coated products, failed to significantly reduce N₂O emissions from a drip-irrigated cotton field in the hyper-arid region of Northwest China. This finding contrasts with numerous studies conducted in humid and sub-humid environments, where EEFs commonly achieve 20–50% reductions in seasonal N₂O fluxes. The ineffectiveness observed here can be attributed to the unique edaphic and hydrological conditions of the study site.

First, the inherently low soil moisture background in this arid region strongly constrains both nitrifier and denitrifier activity. Denitrification, in particular, requires relatively high water-filled pore space (WFPS > 60–70%), a condition rarely met except transiently at the immediate wetting front during or shortly after drip irrigation. Because N₂O production was already substrate- and moisture-limited, slowing nitrification via DCD or controlling release via PCU provided little additional leverage to reduce emissions. The pulse of N₂O following irrigation appeared to be driven by the rapid activation of dormant microbial communities upon wetting rather than by sustained high mineral N availability.

Second, the alkaline soil pH (8.4) likely compromised the efficacy of the nitrification inhibitor DCD. Previous laboratory and field studies have shown that DCD degrades more rapidly at higher pH, reducing its inhibitory duration. In our trial, the early-season divergence in NH₄⁺/NO₃⁻ ratios disappeared within two weeks, suggesting that inhibition was short-lived. For PCU, the release kinetics may have been mismatched with crop demand under the high soil temperature and low humidity of Xinjiang, potentially leading to N release that was either too slow early in the season or too concentrated later, neither of which translated into emission reduction.

Third, the fertigation schedule created frequent but brief episodes of elevated soil moisture. EEFs are designed to modulate N supply over time, but the dominant control on N₂O in this system was the pulsed wetting regime. Because emission events were tightly coupled to irrigation timing and lasted only 48–72 h, the fertilizer type had insufficient differential impact during these narrow windows.

The comparable yields across treatments further indicate that conventional split-application of urea is already well-optimized for this system, leaving little room for EEFs to improve N synchrony or reduce losses. From a mitigation perspective, our results suggest that in arid drip-irrigated cotton systems, management of irrigation quantity and frequency may exert a stronger influence on N₂O emissions than modification of fertilizer chemistry alone. Strategies such as deficit irrigation, alternate partial root-zone drying, or the incorporation of organic amendments to improve soil water holding capacity might offer more viable pathways for emission reduction.

5. Conclusion

In summary, this study found that enhanced efficiency nitrogen fertilizers did not significantly reduce N₂O emissions or increase seed cotton yield compared with conventional urea in a drip-irrigated cotton field in the arid region of Northwest China. The low background emission rates, transient nature of post-irrigation N₂O pulses, and alkaline soil conditions likely limited the efficacy of nitrification inhibitors and controlled-release products. These results imply that the blanket recommendation of EEFs for greenhouse gas mitigation may not be universally applicable across all agro-climatic zones. For hyper-arid, drip-irrigated cropping systems, integrated water-carbon-nutrient management strategies warrant greater attention than fertilizer formulation alone. Further research should explore multi-year datasets and synergistic practices combining optimized irrigation scheduling with novel soil amendments tailored to alkaline, water-limited environments.

title: Effects of midwife-led maternity services on postpartum wellbeing and clinical outcomes in primiparous women under China's one-child policy
text:
Effects of midwife-led maternity services on postpartum wellbeing and clinical outcomes in primiparous women under China’s one-child policy

Abstract

During the final decade of China’s one-child policy, primiparous women faced concentrated familial expectations and heightened childbirth anxiety within an obstetrician-led, highly medicalized maternity system. Midwife-led continuity models were rarely implemented, and their impact in this unique sociocultural context remains under-evaluated. This prospective controlled study compared postpartum wellbeing and clinical outcomes between midwife-led and standard obstetrician-led care. A total of 400 primiparous women were recruited at a tertiary hospital in Shanghai between January 2012 and December 2013; 195 per group completed six-week follow-up. The intervention group received named-midwife continuity care comprising antenatal education, one-to-one intrapartum support, and structured postnatal follow-up. Primary outcomes were Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale

title: Mobilizing social support networks to improve cancer screening: the COACH randomized controlled trial study design
text:
Background: Despite established guidelines, adherence to breast, cervical, and colorectal cancer screening remains suboptimal. Social support networks represent a promising yet underutilized lever to promote screening behaviors, but rigorous trial evidence is lacking.

Objective: To present the study design of the COACH randomized controlled trial, which evaluates whether mobilizing social support networks improves completion of guideline-concordant cancer screening.

Methods: COACH is a multicenter, two-arm, parallel-group randomized controlled trial. Adults overdue for age-appropriate cancer screening will be randomized to receive either a structured social support network mobilization intervention or usual care. The intervention integrates network mapping, peer navigator engagement, and barrier-reduction strategies to activate existing social ties. The primary outcome is completion of targeted cancer screening within 12 months post-randomization. Secondary outcomes include screening intention, perceived social support, and cost-effectiveness.

Conclusion: The COACH trial will provide robust evidence on the efficacy of social network mobilization for increasing cancer screening uptake. If effective, this scalable, low-cost approach could be broadly implemented to enhance early detection and reduce cancer mortality.

title: Inactivation of Escherichia coli O157:H7 and Bacillus cereus by power ultrasound during the curing processing in brining liquid and beef
text:
Inactivation of *Escherichia coli* O157:H7 and *Bacillus cereus* by power ultrasound during the curing processing in brining liquid and beef

Abstract

This study investigated the efficacy of power ultrasound (US) in inactivating *Escherichia coli* O157:H7 and *Bacillus cereus* during the curing of beef. Samples of brining liquid and inoculated beef cubes were subjected to US at 0, 200, 400, and 600 W (20 kHz) for up to 90 min while temperature was maintained below 22 °C. Microbial counts were determined on selective agars. Results showed that US treatment significantly reduced populations of both pathogens in a power- and time-dependent manner (*p* < 0.05). In brine, 600 W for 90 min achieved reductions of 2.8 and 2.1 log CFU/mL for *E. coli* O157:H7 and *B. cereus*, respectively. In beef, the corresponding reductions were 1.9 and 1.3 log CFU/g. *B. cereus* exhibited greater resistance than *E. coli* O157:H7. These findings suggest that power US can enhance the microbiological safety of cured beef, although its efficacy is moderated by the food matrix.

Keywords: Power ultrasound; *Escherichia coli* O157:H7; *Bacillus cereus*; Curing; Beef; Non-thermal inactivation

1. Introduction

Beef curing is a traditional preservation process widely used to enhance flavor, texture, and shelf life. However, the brining environment can support the survival of pathogenic bacteria, posing significant food safety risks. Among these, *Escherichia coli* O157:H7 and *Bacillus cereus* are of particular concern due to their association with severe foodborne illness and their ability to persist in meat-processing environments. Conventional curing relies primarily on salt diffusion, reduced water activity, and low temperature to inhibit microbial growth, yet these hurdles alone may be insufficient to inactivate established pathogen populations.

Power ultrasound (US) is an emerging non-thermal technology that generates acoustic cavitation, producing localized high temperatures, pressures, and reactive oxygen species capable of disrupting microbial cell membranes and denaturing intracellular components. While US has demonstrated antimicrobial efficacy in liquid foods, its application during the curing of solid muscle foods remains underexplored. The heterogeneous matrix of beef and the presence of curing brine create a complex system where acoustic energy distribution and cavitation intensity may vary substantially. Therefore, this study aimed to evaluate the inactivation kinetics of *E. coli* O157:H7 and *B. cereus* by power US applied during the curing process in both brining liquid and beef matrices.

2. Materials and Methods

*Bacterial strains and inoculum preparation.* Pure cultures of *E. coli* O157:H7 (ATCC 43895) and *B. cereus* (ATCC 14579) were activated in Tryptic Soy Broth (TSB) at 37 °C for 24 h. Harvested cells were washed twice with sterile peptone water (0.1%, w/v) and resuspended to approximately 10^7 CFU/mL.

*Sample preparation.* A curing brine was formulated containing 10% (w/v) NaCl, 1% (w/v) sugar, and 0.3% (w/v) sodium nitrite. Fresh beef (*M. semitendinosus*) was trimmed of visible fat and cut into 2 × 2 × 2 cm cubes. Beef cubes were surface-inoculated by immersion in the bacterial suspension for 15 min and drained for 5 min to achieve an initial load of approximately 7.0 log CFU/g. Inoculated brining liquid (initial load ~7.0 log CFU/mL) and inoculated beef cubes were separately packaged in sterile polyethylene bags; meat samples were fully immersed in 100 mL of fresh uninoculated brine to simulate actual curing conditions.

*Ultrasound treatment.* Samples were treated in a circulating water bath connected to an ultrasonic generator operating at a fixed frequency of 20 kHz and nominal power settings of 0 (control), 200, 400, and 600 W for 30, 60, and 90 min. The temperature of the medium was monitored with a thermocouple and maintained below 22 °C by circulating iced water to preclude thermal inactivation.

*Microbiological analysis.* After treatment, brine samples were directly serially diluted in sterile peptone water. Beef cubes were stomached with 100 mL peptone water for 2 min. Appropriate dilutions were plated onto Sorbitol MacConkey Agar (*E. coli* O157:H7) and Mannitol Egg Yolk Polymyxin Agar (*B. cereus*), incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. Counts were expressed as log CFU/mL or log CFU/g.

*Statistical analysis.* All experiments were performed in triplicate and arranged in a completely randomized design. Data were analyzed by two-way ANOVA using SPSS 26.0, with Tukey’s post-hoc test to compare means. Significant differences were determined at *p* < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

In brining liquid, US treatment induced significant reductions in both pathogens compared with non-sonicated controls (*p* < 0.05). After 90 min, *E. coli* O157:H7 populations decreased by 1.1, 1.9, and 2.8 log CFU/mL at 200, 400, and 600 W, respectively. For *B. cereus*, reductions of 0.8, 1.4, and 2.1 log CFU/mL were observed under equivalent conditions. The inactivation efficiency increased markedly with acoustic power and treatment duration.

In beef, the antimicrobial efficacy of US was comparatively lower. Treatment at 600 W for 90 min reduced *E. coli* O157:H7 and *B. cereus* by 1.9 and 1.3 log CFU/g, respectively. At 400 W, reductions were 1.2 and 0.7 log CFU/g after 90 min, whereas 200 W produced negligible effects (<0.5 log). These results indicate that the solid food matrix attenuates ultrasonic energy transmission and dampens cavitation intensity. Throughout all treatments, *B. cereus* demonstrated higher resistance to US than *E. coli* O157:H7. No significant temperature rise (>3 °C), pH shift, or color change was recorded between control and treated samples (*p* > 0.05), confirming that the observed inactivation was predominantly attributable to non-thermal cavitation effects.

4. Discussion

The present findings demonstrate that power US can effectively reduce *E. coli* O157:H7 and *B. cereus* during beef curing, though efficacy is strongly influenced by the treatment medium. The superior inactivation observed in brining liquid can be attributed to unimpeded acoustic cavitation, where the violent collapse of bubbles generates intense shear forces, micro-streaming, and free radicals that compromise cell membrane integrity. Conversely, the heterogeneous structure of beef—characterized by dense muscle fibers, connective tissue, and entrapped air—scatters and absorbs acoustic energy, thereby diminishing localized cavitation intensity at bacterial cell surfaces. Additionally, proteins and lipids released from beef may stabilize bacterial membranes or scavenge free radicals, further protecting embedded pathogens.

The greater tolerance of *B. cereus* relative to *E. coli* O157:H7 aligns with previous reports highlighting the structural resilience of Gram-positive bacteria and their robust cell walls. Although the reductions achieved in beef (1.3–1.9 log) are modest compared to thermal pasteurization, they represent a meaningful enhancement in microbial safety when integrated into a hurdle strategy alongside curing salts and refrigeration. Future research should optimize US parameters in combination with mild heat or natural antimicrobials to improve lethal penetration while preserving beef quality attributes. Industrial implementation would also require scale-up studies to ensure uniform acoustic field distribution in large brining tanks.

5. Conclusion

Power ultrasound significantly inactivated *E. coli* O157:H7 and *B. cereus* during the curing process, with efficacy increasing as a function of acoustic power and treatment time. Inactivation was more pronounced in brining liquid than in beef, and *B. cereus* exhibited greater resistance than *E. coli* O157:H7. These results support the potential of power US as an auxiliary non-thermal intervention to improve the microbiological safety of cured beef products.

title: Synthesis of attapulgite/N-isopropylacrylamide and its use in drug release
text: Stimuli-responsive drug delivery systems have attracted considerable attention for their ability to release therapeutic agents in a controlled manner. Among various smart polymers, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM) is particularly promising due to its lower critical solution temperature (LCST) close to physiological conditions, enabling temperature-triggered drug release. However, pure PNIPAM hydrogels often suffer from poor mechanical properties and rapid burst release, which limit their practical applications. To overcome these drawbacks, the incorporation of natural clay minerals as reinforcing fillers has emerged as an effective strategy. Attapulgite, a hydrated magnesium aluminum silicate with unique fibrous morphology, abundant surface hydroxyl groups, and excellent biocompatibility, offers great potential for developing high-performance organic–inorganic hybrid materials. In this study, we report the facile synthesis of an attapulgite/PNIPAM nanocomposite through in situ free-radical polymerization. The chemical structure, morphology, and thermal responsiveness of the obtained materials were systematically characterized. Furthermore, their application as temperature-sensitive drug carriers was investigated using a model drug. This work presents a promising approach for constructing clay-based smart delivery platforms with improved mechanical strength and controlled release behavior.

title: Perceived Factors Influencing the Public Intention to Use E-Consultation: Analysis of Web-Based Survey Data
text: The survey yielded 514 responses; after excluding 32 incomplete records, the final sample comprised 482 participants. Respondents were predominantly female (58.3%) with a mean age of 34.2 (SD = 11.4) years. Hierarchical multiple regression showed that the model accounted for 61% of the variance in intention to use e-consultation (R² = .61, F(5, 476) = 148.32, p < .001). Perceived usefulness was the strongest predictor (β = .42, p < .001), followed by perceived ease of use (β = .28, p < .001) and trust in data security (β = .19, p < .01). Perceived risk exerted a significant negative effect (β = –.15, p < .05), whereas social influence and facilitating conditions were non-significant (p > .05). These results align with established technology acceptance frameworks, emphasizing that utilitarian and trust-related factors outweigh social pressures in digital health contexts. The adverse impact of perceived risk highlights the importance of transparent privacy policies and robust cybersecurity measures. Although the cross-sectional design precludes causal claims, the findings suggest that enhancing system utility, simplifying user interfaces, and strengthening data protection are essential to promoting public uptake of e-consultation.

title: Bio-organic fertilizer with reduced rates of chemical fertilization improves soil fertility and enhances tomato yield and quality
text:
Bio-organic fertilizer with reduced rates of chemical fertilization improves soil fertility and enhances tomato yield and quality

Abstract

Excessive chemical fertilization in intensive tomato production has led to soil degradation and declining fruit quality. This study investigated the effects of partial substitution of chemical fertilizer with bio-organic fertilizer (BOF) on soil properties, yield, and fruit quality of tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum* L.). A field experiment was conducted with four treatments: conventional chemical fertilizer (CF), 30 % reduced chemical fertilizer (RF), 30 % reduced chemical fertilizer plus BOF (RF+BOF), and BOF alone. Results showed that the RF+BOF treatment significantly increased soil organic matter, total nitrogen, available phosphorus, and microbial populations compared with CF. Notably, RF+BOF maintained comparable yield to CF and significantly improved fruit soluble solids, vitamin C, lycopene content, and sugar-acid ratio. These findings suggest that integrating BOF with reduced chemical fertilization is an effective strategy for sustainable tomato production.

Keywords: Bio-organic fertilizer; Chemical fertilization reduction; Tomato; Soil fertility; Yield; Fruit quality

1. Introduction

Tomato (*Solanum lycopersicum* L.) is one of the most economically important vegetable crops worldwide. To maximize yield, intensive production systems often rely heavily on chemical fertilizers, which gradually induce soil acidification, organic matter depletion, and imbalance of soil microbial communities. In recent years, the concept of chemical fertilizer reduction has gained increasing attention as a pathway toward greener agriculture. However, simply reducing mineral nutrient inputs without alternatives frequently results in yield penalties.

Bio-organic fertilizer (BOF), produced by inoculating specific functional microorganisms into decomposed organic substrates, has been reported to enhance nutrient availability, suppress soil-borne pathogens, and improve soil physical structure. Although previous studies have documented the beneficial effects of BOF on crop performance, limited information is available regarding its synergistic application with reduced chemical fertilization rates in tomato cultivation. It remains unclear whether BOF can compensate for reduced mineral fertilizer inputs while simultaneously improving soil fertility and fruit quality. Therefore, the objective of this study was to evaluate the integrated effects of BOF application coupled with 30 % chemical fertilizer reduction on soil biochemical properties, tomato yield, and fruit quality in a field setting.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Experimental site and design

A field experiment was conducted from March to July 2023 at the experimental farm of Shandong Academy of Agricultural Sciences (36°42′ N, 117°09′ E), China. The soil was a loam texture with the following baseline characteristics (0–20 cm): pH 7.2, organic matter 18.5 g kg⁻¹, total nitrogen (TN) 1.12 g kg⁻¹, available phosphorus (AP) 21.8 mg kg⁻¹, and available potassium (AK) 158.0 mg kg⁻¹.

A randomized complete block design with three replicates was employed. Each plot measured 5 m × 4 m (20 m²) with a 1 m buffer zone. Four treatments were established: (1) conventional chemical fertilizer (CF), supplying N 300, P₂O₅ 150, and K₂O 225 kg ha⁻¹; (2) reduced chemical fertilizer by 30 % (RF), supplying N 210, P₂O₅ 105, and K₂O 157.5 kg ha⁻¹; (3) reduced chemical fertilizer plus bio-organic fertilizer (RF+BOF), identical to RF for chemical inputs plus 3 000 kg ha⁻¹ of commercial BOF containing *Bacillus subtilis* and *Trichoderma harzianum* (organic matter ≥ 45 %, total N-P₂O₅-K₂O ≥ 5 %); and (4) BOF alone at 6 000 kg ha⁻¹ without chemical fertilizer. The tomato cultivar “Zhongza 9” was transplanted on March 18 at a density of 45 000 plants ha⁻¹. Standard irrigation and pest management practices were applied uniformly across all plots.

2.2. Sampling and measurements

At harvest, five representative plants per plot were randomly selected to record fruit number per plant and average fruit weight. Plot yields were converted to hectare-level yields (t ha⁻¹).

Soil samples (0–20 cm) were collected from each plot using a five-point composite sampling method. One portion was stored at 4 °C for microbial analysis. The remainder was air-dried and passed through a 2 mm sieve for chemical analysis. Soil pH was measured with a glass electrode in a 1:2.5 soil-to-water suspension. Soil organic matter (SOM) was determined by potassium dichromate oxidation. TN was analyzed via the Kjeldahl method. AP was extracted with sodium bicarbonate and quantified colorimetrically. AK was extracted with ammonium acetate and measured by flame photometry. Soil bacteria, fungi, and actinomycetes were enumerated using the plate-count technique on beef extract peptone, Martin’s, and Gause’s No. 1 media, respectively.

Fruit quality was assessed at the breaker stage. Soluble solids content (TSS) was measured with a digital refractometer. Vitamin C (Vc) content was determined by 2,6-dichlorophenol indophenol titration. Lycopene was extracted with acetone-hexane and measured spectrophotometrically. Titratable acidity (TA) was titrated with 0.1 mol L⁻¹ NaOH and expressed as citric acid percentage. The sugar-to-acid ratio was calculated as TSS divided by TA.

2.3. Statistical analysis

All data were subjected to one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) using SPSS 26.0. Significant differences among treatment means were separated by Duncan’s multiple range test at *P* < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1. Soil fertility and microbial properties

Compared with CF, the RF+BOF treatment significantly increased SOM by 19.8 % (21.7 vs. 18.1 g kg⁻¹), TN by 15.3 % (1.36 vs. 1.18 g kg⁻¹), AP by 23.4 % (38.5 vs. 31.2 mg kg⁻¹), and AK by 9.4 % (168 vs. 154 mg kg⁻¹) (*P* < 0.05; Table 1). The BOF-only treatment exhibited the highest SOM (23.4 g kg⁻¹) but the lowest mineral nutrient concentrations among all treatments. Soil pH remained relatively stable across treatments, ranging from 7.0 to 7.2.

Table 1 Effects of different fertilization regimes on soil chemical properties.

| Treatment | pH | SOM (g kg⁻¹) | TN (g kg⁻¹) | AP (mg kg⁻¹) | AK (mg kg⁻¹) |
|-----------|----|--------------|-------------|--------------|--------------|
| CF        | 7.0a | 18.1c | 1.18c | 31.2c | 154b |
| RF        | 7.1a | 17.5c | 1.10d | 26.8d | 148b |
| RF+BOF    | 7.1a | 21.7b | 1.36b | 38.5b | 168a |
| BOF       | 7.2a | 23.4a | 1.45a | 24.5d | 142b |

*Note:* Values followed by different lowercase letters within a column differ significantly at *P* < 0.05.

Soil microbial abundance responded markedly to organic amendments. The RF+BOF treatment recorded the highest bacterial count (8.6 × 10⁶ CFU g⁻¹ dry soil), which was 2.1-fold greater than that under CF (4.1 × 10⁶ CFU g⁻¹). Similarly, fungal and actinomycete populations in RF+BOF increased by 56.4 % and 48.7 %, respectively, relative to CF. The RF treatment alone showed the lowest microbial counts among all treatments.

3.2. Tomato yield

Yield parameters varied significantly among treatments (*P* < 0.05; Table 2). The RF+BOF treatment achieved a yield of 94.8 t ha⁻¹, which was statistically comparable to the CF yield of 92.5 t ha⁻¹ and significantly higher than the RF yield of 81.3 t ha⁻¹. The BOF-only treatment produced the lowest yield (76.4 t ha⁻¹). Average fruit weight in RF+BOF reached 188.4 g, exceeding that of CF (174.2 g) by 8.2 %.

Table 2 Effects of different fertilization regimes on tomato yield components.

| Treatment | Fruit number per plant | Fruit weight (g) | Yield (t ha⁻¹) |
|-----------|------------------------|------------------|----------------|
| CF        | 11.8b | 174.2b | 92.5a |
| RF        | 10.2c | 162.4c | 81.3b |
| RF+BOF    | 12.5a | 188.4a | 94.8a |
| BOF       | 9.5c | 156.8c | 76.4b |

*Note:* Values followed by different lowercase letters within a column differ significantly at *P* < 0.05.

3.3. Fruit quality

Fruit quality was substantially enhanced under the RF+BOF regime (Table 3). TSS increased from 4.3 % in CF to 5.7 % in RF+BOF. Vc content rose by 29.3 % (28.4 vs. 22.0 mg 100 g⁻¹ fresh weight), and lycopene content increased by 39.1 % (4.2 vs. 3.0 mg 100 g⁻¹). Although TA showed a modest increase under RF+BOF (0.41 % vs. 0.36 % in CF), the sugar-to-acid ratio was significantly improved, reaching 13.9 compared with 11.9 in CF. The RF treatment generally resulted in inferior quality attributes relative to CF, whereas BOF alone produced the highest TSS and Vc but lower overall yield.

Table 3 Effects of different fertilization regimes on tomato fruit quality.

| Treatment | TSS (%) | Vc (mg 100 g⁻¹) | Lycopene (mg 100 g⁻¹) | TA (%) | Sugar-acid ratio |
|-----------|---------|-----------------|-----------------------|--------|------------------|
| CF        | 4.3c | 22.0c | 3.0c | 0.36b | 11.9b |
| RF        | 3.8d | 19.5d | 2.6d | 0.38b | 10.0c |
| RF+BOF    | 5.7b | 28.4b | 4.2b | 0.41a | 13.9a |
| BOF       | 6.1a | 31.2a | 4.5a | 0.43a | 14.2a |

*Note:* Values followed by different lowercase letters within a column differ significantly at *P* < 0.05.

4. Discussion

The present study demonstrates that a 30 % reduction in chemical fertilizer coupled with BOF application not only maintained tomato yield but also significantly improved soil fertility and fruit quality. The enhancement of SOM, TN, and AP under RF+BOF can be attributed to the combined effects of external organic substrate input and the presence of plant-growth-promoting microorganisms. *Bacillus* and *Trichoderma* species in the BOF are known to solubilize insoluble phosphate, fix atmospheric nitrogen, and accelerate organic matter mineralization, thereby replenishing the nutrient pool that was reduced by cutting chemical inputs.

The increased microbial biomass and community diversity in the RF+BOF treatment further indicate a restoration of soil biological function. Intensive chemical fertilization often suppresses soil microbial activity through osmotic stress and pH alteration. By contrast, the introduction of BOF provided readily available carbon sources and beneficial microflora, creating a more favorable rhizosphere environment. This likely improved root architecture and nutrient uptake efficiency, which compensated for the lower mineral fertilizer rate and sustained high productivity.

The superior fruit quality observed under RF+BOF—particularly the elevated lycopene and Vc contents—suggests that organic amendments regulate secondary metabolism in tomato plants. Balanced nutrient availability, especially moderate nitrogen levels combined with improved micronutrient mobilization by microbial symbionts, may enhance antioxidant synthesis and sugar accumulation. The slight increase in TA under organic treatments contributed to a more balanced flavor profile, as reflected in the higher sugar-acid ratio.

It is noteworthy that BOF alone failed to match the yields of CF and RF+BOF. This implies that while BOF can enrich soil health, the nutrient release rate from organic materials may be insufficient to meet the high nutrient demand during peak tomato fruit development. Therefore, integrating reduced chemical fertilizer with BOF appears to offer an optimal synchrony between rapid nutrient supply and long-term soil conditioning.

5. Conclusion

In conclusion, substituting 30 % of conventional chemical fertilizer with bio-organic fertilizer represents a viable agronomic strategy for tomato production. This integrated approach improved soil organic matter status, enhanced microbial abundance, maintained high marketable yield, and markedly increased fruit nutritional and flavor quality. These results provide practical support for fertilizer reduction policies and the sustainable intensification of protected vegetable cropping systems.

title: Therapeutic effect of Xuebijing combined with thymosin on hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome: A protocol of systematic review and meta-analysis
text:
Therapeutic effect of Xuebijing combined with thymosin on hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome: A protocol of systematic review and meta-analysis

Abstract

Background: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) remains a life-threatening zoonosis with limited specific therapies. Xuebijing injection and thymosin formulations have shown individual immunomodulatory and organ-protective benefits, yet the efficacy and safety of their combined use in HFRS remain unclear.

Objective: This protocol describes a systematic review and meta-analysis to evaluate the therapeutic effects of Xuebijing plus thymosin in patients with HFRS.

Methods: We will search PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed from inception to 31 December 2024 for randomized controlled trials (RCTs). Primary outcomes include all-cause mortality and time to oliguria resolution; secondary outcomes encompass renal function recovery, platelet normalization, length of hospital stay, and adverse events. Risk of bias will be assessed with the Cochrane RoB 2 tool, and meta-analysis will be conducted using RevMan 5.4 with a random-effects model.

Results: A pilot search retrieved 147 records. After duplicate removal and screening, eight RCTs enrolling 623 participants appear eligible. All trials were conducted in China (2015–2023), with sample sizes ranging from 58 to 96. Intervention arms used Xuebijing (50–100 mL/day) combined with thymosin α1 (1.6 mg subcutaneously) or thymopeptides (20–60 mg/day) alongside conventional therapy.

Conclusion: This review will provide synthesized evidence to guide adjuvant therapy decisions in HFRS.

Keywords: Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome; Xuebijing; Thymosin; Systematic review; Meta-analysis; Protocol

---

Introduction

Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused primarily by Hantaan virus and Seoul virus, is a severe rodent-borne disease endemic across East Asia and parts of Europe. Characterized by fever, capillary leakage, hemorrhagic manifestations, and acute kidney injury, HFRS carries substantial morbidity and mortality even with modern supportive care. Current management remains largely symptomatic, encompassing fluid resuscitation, electrolyte correction, ribavirin, and renal replacement therapy when indicated; no universally accepted immunomodulatory regimen exists to attenuate disease progression.

Xuebijing injection, a compounded traditional Chinese medicine containing bioactive extracts from *Carthamus tinctorius*, *Paeonia lactiflora*, and other herbs, exhibits anti-inflammatory, anticoagulant, and endothelial-protective properties. It is widely used in China for sepsis and severe infectious diseases. Thymosin α1 and related thymic peptides enhance T-lymphocyte maturation, restore adaptive immunity, and modulate cytokine networks, suggesting potential utility in viral illnesses characterized by immune dysregulation. Theoretically, combining Xuebijing’s dampening of systemic inflammation with thymosin’s immune restoration could attenuate the “cytokine storm” and hasten renal recovery in HFRS. Over the past decade, several small randomized controlled trials (RCTs) have explored this combination; however, individual studies are underpowered, employ heterogeneous endpoints, and lack independent replication. Consequently, clinicians lack definitive evidence to adopt this dual adjuvant strategy. This protocol outlines a systematic review and meta-analysis designed to rigorously synthesize available RCT evidence, clarify clinical efficacy, and inform treatment guidelines for HFRS.

---

Materials and Methods

This protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD4202456789) and will be reported in accordance with the PRISMA-P 2015 statement.

Eligibility criteria. We will include RCTs and quasi-RCTs enrolling patients of any age with laboratory-confirmed HFRS (serology or PCR). The intervention group must receive Xuebijing injection combined with any thymosin formulation (e.g., thymosin α1 or thymopeptides) alongside conventional therapy. Controls will receive conventional therapy alone or with placebo. Primary outcomes are all-cause mortality during hospitalization and time to oliguria resolution. Secondary outcomes include time to platelet count normalization, serum creatinine recovery, urinary protein clearance, length of hospital stay, and incidence of adverse events. We will exclude animal studies, case reports, reviews, and trials lacking a comparator group.

Information sources and search. We will systematically search PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane CENTRAL, Web of Science, CNKI, Wanfang, VIP, and SinoMed from database inception to 31 December 2024 without language restrictions. A sample PubMed strategy combines MeSH terms—“Hemorrhagic Fever with Renal Syndrome,” “Hantavirus,” “Xuebijing,” “Thymosin,” and “Randomized Controlled Trial”—with corresponding free-text synonyms. Grey literature (dissertations, conference abstracts) and trial registries will be screened, and reference lists of included studies hand-searched to identify additional citations.

Study selection and data extraction. Two reviewers will independently screen titles and abstracts, followed by full-text review, using Rayyan QCRI. Disagreements will be resolved by consensus or arbitration by a third reviewer. A standardized extraction form will capture author/year, country, sample size, participant demographics, disease severity, intervention dosing and duration, and outcome data (means and standard deviations or events and totals).

Risk of bias and evidence certainty. We will use the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias 2 (RoB 2) tool for randomized trials, grading each domain as low risk, some concerns, or high risk. The Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework will appraise the certainty of evidence for each outcome.

Statistical analysis. Meta-analysis will be performed in RevMan 5.4 using a random-effects model. Dichotomous outcomes will be expressed as risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs); continuous outcomes as mean differences (MDs) or standardized mean differences (SMDs) with 95% CIs. Heterogeneity will be quantified via the I² statistic and χ² test; an I² > 50% will prompt exploration of sources through predefined subgroup analyses. Subgroups will include disease severity (mild/moderate vs. severe/critical), thymosin type (α1 vs. peptide), and timing of initiation. Sensitivity analyses will exclude high-risk studies and trials with imputed data. Funnel plots and Egger’s regression test will assess publication bias if at least ten studies are available.

---

Results

A preliminary search conducted on 15 October 2024 identified 147 potentially relevant records: PubMed (n = 12), Embase (n = 18), Cochrane Library (n = 3), Web of Science (n = 5), CNKI (n = 56), Wanfang (n = 31), VIP (n = 15), and SinoMed (n = 7). After removing 43 duplicates, 104 titles and abstracts were screened. Seventy-two records were excluded as irrelevant reviews, case series, or non-comparative studies. Thirty-two full-text articles were retrieved for detailed assessment; 23 were excluded for wrong intervention (n = 8), non-randomized design (n = 10), duplicate publication (n = 3), or unavailable outcome data (n = 2). Consequently, eight RCTs enrolling a total of 623 participants appear eligible for inclusion.

All identified trials were conducted in China between 2015 and 2023. Individual study samples ranged from 58 to 96 participants (median 78). Mean participant age ranged from 42 to 51 years, and the proportion of severe or critical cases varied from 25% to 44%. In the intervention arms, Xuebijing was administered intravenously at 50–100 mL daily for 7–14 days, combined with thymosin α1 (1.6 mg subcutaneously every 48–72 hours) or thymopeptides (20–60 mg intravenously daily). Control groups received conventional therapy including ribavirin, fluid management, and renal replacement as indicated. Seven studies reported platelet recovery time, six reported oliguria duration, five reported serum creatinine normalization, four reported in-hospital mortality, and three documented adverse events. A pilot assessment of risk of bias indicated three studies at low risk, three with some concerns (primarily around allocation concealment), and two at high risk due to lack of blinding and selective outcome reporting.

---

Discussion

This protocol outlines the first systematic review specifically examining the combination of Xuebijing and thymosin for HFRS.
