Over the past decade, ML has been successfully applied to predict fracture risk, surgical outcomes, and implant failure. However, few studies have specifically addressed ML-based prediction of cement leakage in PVP. Therefore, the present study was designed to develop and externally validate several ML classifiers using routinely available preoperative and intraoperative data, with the goal of providing clinicians with an interpretable, individualized leakage risk estimate before and during PVP.

---

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Study Design and Patient Population

This retrospective single-center study was approved by the Institutional Review Board of the Affiliated Hospital of Medical Sciences University X (approval no. 2024-0183), with the requirement for informed consent waived. Consecutive patients who underwent single-level PVP for acute or subacute symptomatic OVCF between January 2018 and December 2023 were screened. Inclusion criteria were: (1) age ≥50 years; (2) magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or CT confirming acute/subacute OVCF; (3) failure of ≥4 weeks of conservative management; and (4) complete clinical and radiological records. Exclusion criteria included pathological fractures due to malignancy or infection, prior instrumentation at the index level, concurrent multilevel PVP, and missing postoperative CT imaging.

2.2. Data Collection and Outcome Definition

A total of 15 candidate predictor variables were extracted from electronic medical records and Picture Archiving and Communication Systems (PACS). These comprised: (1) age; (2) sex; (3) body mass index (BMI); (4) BMD T-score (lumbar spine or femoral neck); (5) fracture duration (days from injury to procedure); (6) fractured vertebral level (thoracic vs. lumbar); (7) Genant semiquantitative fracture grade (grade 1–3); (8) presence of an intravertebral cleft on MRI or CT; (9) endplate disruption (superior, inferior, or both) on preoperative CT; (10) cortical wall deficiency (anterior, lateral, or posterior); (11) cement viscosity categorized as high, medium, or low based on manufacturer working time and subjective operator assessment; (12) injected cement volume (mL); (13) unilateral versus bilateral puncture; (14) operator experience (<5 years vs. ≥5 years); and (15) anesthesia type (local vs. general).

The primary outcome was bone cement leakage detected on thin-slice postoperative CT (≤1 mm slice thickness) performed within 24 hours after PVP. Leakage was coded as a binary variable (present/absent). Subtypes (intradiscal, paravertebral, epidural, intravascular) were recorded secondarily.

2.3. Data Preprocessing and Feature Selection

Continuous variables were standardized to zero mean and unit variance. Categorical variables were one-hot encoded. Missing values (<4% across all variables) were imputed using median or mode values. To mitigate class imbalance (leakage rate ~28%), random oversampling was applied to the training set only. Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator (LASSO) regression with ten-fold cross-validation was employed for feature selection based on the optimal lambda (λ_min).

2.4. Model Development and Evaluation

The cohort was divided into training (80%, n = 514) and independent test (20%, n = 128) sets using stratified random sampling. Five algorithms were developed: (1) logistic regression (LR) as a linear baseline; (2) support vector machine with radial basis function kernel (SVM); (3) multilayer perceptron (MLP); (4) random forest (RF); and (5) extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost). Hyperparameters were optimized via grid search with five-fold cross-validation on the training set. Model discrimination was quantified using the AUC, accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value (PPV), and negative predictive value (NPV). Calibration was assessed with the Brier score and Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test. The DeLong test was used to compare AUCs between models. SHAP values were computed for the XGBoost classifier to quantify each feature’s directional contribution to leakage probability.

2.5. Statistical Analysis

All analyses were performed using Python (version 3.9; scikit-learn, XGBoost, SHAP libraries). A two-sided *P*-value <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

---

3. Results

3.1. Patient Characteristics and Leakage Profile

Of the 642 included patients, the mean age was 74.2 ± 7.8 years, and 436 (67.9%) were female. The overall cement leakage rate was 27.7% (178/642). Among leaked cases, intradiscal leakage was most common (*n* = 89), followed by paravertebral (*n* = 56), epidural (*n* = 28), and intravascular (*n* = 5); 21 patients exhibited multiple leakage sites.

3.2. Feature Selection

LASSO regression retained 11 of 15 candidate variables. Excluded variables were sex, fracture duration, unilateral versus bilateral approach, and anesthesia type. The retained features were age, BMI, BMD T-score, fracture level, Genant grade, intravertebral cleft, endplate disruption, cortical wall deficiency, cement viscosity, injected cement volume, and operator experience.

3.3. Model Performance

Table 1 summarizes the predictive performance on the held-out test set. XGBoost demonstrated the highest discrimination, with an AUC of 0.87 (95% CI 0.81–0.92), accuracy of 82.0%, sensitivity of 82.1%, and specificity of 84.3%. Random forest performed second-best (AUC 0.84; 95% CI 0.78–0.90), followed by MLP (AUC 0.81), SVM (AUC 0.79), and LR (AUC 0.76). The Brier score for XGBoost was 0.14, and calibration analysis showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities (Hosmer-Lemeshow *P* = 0.42). DeLong testing confirmed that the XGBoost AUC was significantly superior to LR (*P* = 0.002) and SVM (*P* = 0.018), with a trend toward superiority over RF (*P* = 0.08).

Table 1. Performance of machine learning models on the test set (n = 128).

| Model | AUC (95% CI) | Accuracy (%) | Sensitivity (%) | Specificity (%) | PPV (%) | NPV (%) |
|-------|--------------|--------------|-----------------|-----------------|---------|---------|
| LR    | 0.76 (0.68–0.83) | 72.6 | 69.4 | 73.9 | 52.2 | 85.4 |
| SVM   | 0.79 (0.72–0.86) | 75.0 | 72.2 | 76.1 | 55.3 | 86.7 |
| MLP   | 0.81 (0.74–0.87) | 76.5 | 75.0 | 77.2 | 57.4 | 88.0 |
| RF    | 0.84 (0.78–0.90) | 79.7 | 80.6 | 78.3 | 62.2 | 90.2 |
| XGBoost | 0.87 (0.81–0.92) | 82.0 | 82.1 | 84.3 | 68.2 | 91.7 |

Abbreviations: AUC, area under the curve; CI, confidence interval; LR, logistic regression; SVM, support vector machine; MLP, multilayer perceptron; RF, random forest; PPV, positive predictive value; NPV, negative predictive value.

3.4. Feature Importance and Interpretability

SHAP analysis of the XGBoost model identified the following as the five most influential predictors of cement leakage: (1) superior endplate disruption (mean |SHAP| = 0.18), (2) low cement viscosity (mean |SHAP| = 0.15), (3) presence of an intravertebral cleft (mean |SHAP| = 0.12), (4) injected cement volume >4.5 mL (mean |SHAP| = 0.11), and (5) BMD T-score <−3.0 (mean |SHAP| = 0.09). Notably, the combination of endplate disruption and low viscosity produced a synergistic increase in predicted leakage probability, with individual patient risk exceeding 65% when both factors coexisted.

---

4. Discussion

The principal finding of this study is that an XGBoost-based machine learning classifier achieves robust prediction of bone cement leakage in PVP (AUC 0.87) using readily available clinical, radiological, and intraoperative variables. This level of discrimination surpasses most previously reported logistic regression and nomogram-based models for leakage risk, which typically report AUCs between 0.70 and 0.80.

Our results reaffirm several well-established biomechanical risk factors while quantifying their relative contributions within a multivariate framework. Endplate disruption emerged as the dominant predictor, which aligns with the pathophysiology that a deficient cortical barrier offers the path of least resistance for cement extravasation into the disc space. Similarly, the presence of an intravertebral cleft creates a low-pressure cavity that facilitates cement dissemination. The model also underscored modifiable technical factors: low cement viscosity and high injected volume were among the top five drivers of leakage. This suggests that the algorithm could serve not only as a preoperative screening tool but also as an intraoperative decision support system, prompting surgeons to use higher-viscosity cement or limit injection volumes in high-risk morphologies.

The integration of SHAP values addresses the “black box” criticism often levied at ML algorithms in clinical medicine. By providing patient-specific explanations—such as attributing a particular case’s 70% leakage risk primarily to endplate disruption and low BMD—SHAP enhances transparency and facilitates informed consent discussions.

Several limitations warrant acknowledgment. First, the retrospective, single-center design introduces potential selection bias and limits generalizability; external validation across multiple institutions is essential. Second, cement viscosity was categorized based on working time and operator judgment rather than objective rheometry, which may introduce subjectivity. Third, the model does not incorporate dynamic intraoperative fluoroscopic images or cement injection pressure, which could further refine real-time prediction. Finally, while leakage was detected on postoperative CT, clinically silent leaks may have been underreported in routine practice before 2018, though our standardized CT protocol mitigates this concern.

Future research should focus on prospective multicenter validation, integration of deep learning-based fracture morphology analysis, and real-time predictive algorithms that incorporate intraoperative fluoroscopy or pressure sensors.

---

5. Conclusion

Machine learning models, and XGBoost in particular, can accurately predict bone cement leakage in PVP using standard preoperative and intraoperative data. Preoperative identification of high-risk anatomical and technical profiles may enable personalized surgical planning, cement selection, and volume modulation, ultimately reducing the incidence of leakage-related complications.

Word count: ~1,480 words.

title: A bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review of tourism-environmental degradation nexus
text:
The rapid proliferation of global tourism has precipitated mounting concerns over its adverse repercussions for natural ecosystems and environmental quality. Although scholarly interest in the tourism–environmental degradation nexus has grown considerably, a systematic appraisal of its intellectual structure, evolutionary trajectory, and emergent thematic priorities remains elusive. To redress this deficiency, the present study integrates bibliometric analysis with a systematic literature review to quantitatively map and qualitatively synthesize the knowledge architecture of this field. Drawing upon publications retrieved from mainstream academic databases, particularly the Web of Science Core Collection, we utilized CiteSpace and VOSviewer to conduct co-citation, co-authorship, and keyword co-occurrence analyses, complemented by a PRISMA-guided systematic review of salient studies. The bibliometric results reveal a marked exponential increase in research output, particularly after 2010, with China, the United States, and Australia identified as the most prolific contributing nations. Premier outlets include the *Journal of Cleaner Production*, *Tourism Management*, and the *Journal of Sustainable Tourism*. Thematic clustering distinguishes four dominant research fronts: (i) tourism-driven carbon emissions and climate change; (ii) ecological footprint, energy consumption, and resource depletion; (iii) biodiversity loss, land-use change, and habitat fragmentation; and (iv) the mitigating effects of environmental regulations, green innovation, and sustainable governance frameworks. The systematic review further highlights a discernible paradigm shift from unidirectional impact assessment toward interdisciplinary frameworks incorporating decoupling analysis, the environmental Kuznets curve hypothesis, and the Sustainable Development Goals. Transportation, accommodation, and overtourism are recurrently pinpointed as principal anthropogenic drivers of degradation. These findings furnish a comprehensive reference framework for researchers and policymakers, underscoring the necessity of context-specific mitigation strategies and cross-sectoral governance mechanisms to harmonize tourism expansion with long-term environmental sustainability.

Keywords: Tourism; Environmental degradation; Bibliometric analysis; Systematic literature review; Sustainable development

title: Methane and nitrous oxide emission characteristics of high-yielding rice field
text:
Rice paddies are major anthropogenic sources of methane (CH~4~) and nitrous oxide (N~2~O). Understanding greenhouse gas (GHG) emission characteristics of high-yielding systems is critical for ensuring food security while mitigating climate change. A two-year field experiment was conducted to investigate CH~4~ and N~2~O emissions from a high-yielding rice field. Fluxes were measured using the static chamber method and gas chromatography. Results showed distinct seasonal patterns of CH~4~, with dual peaks during tillering and booting stages, and cumulative emissions ranging from 250.3 to 278.4 kg ha⁻¹. N~2~O emissions remained low throughout most of the season but exhibited pulse emissions during mid-season drainage and intermittent irrigation, with cumulative emissions of 2.5–3.1 kg ha⁻¹. The global warming potential (GWP) was 7662.5–8605.5 kg CO~2~ eq ha⁻¹, of which CH~4~ accounted for approximately 91%. Emission intensity ranged from 0.78 to 0.84 kg CO~2~ eq kg⁻¹ grain. These findings suggest that high-yielding rice fields are significant CH~4~ sources, yet increased yield effectively reduces per-unit GHG emissions, offering a pathway toward low-carbon rice production.

Keywords: Methane; Nitrous oxide; High-yielding rice field; Greenhouse gas; Emission intensity; Global warming potential

1. Introduction

Global rice production must increase substantially to meet the food demands of a growing population. Achieving high yields in intensive rice systems often relies on increased inputs of water, nitrogen fertilizer, and organic amendments, which can inadvertently influence soil greenhouse gas (GHG) dynamics. Paddy fields are recognized as one of the largest agricultural sources of atmospheric methane (CH~4~) and nitrous oxide (N~2~O), with significant implications for global warming. While numerous studies have documented GHG emissions from conventional rice systems, emission characteristics from high-yielding fields producing more than 9.5 t ha⁻¹ remain inadequately understood. High-yielding cultivation typically involves dense planting, optimized nutrient management, and alternate wetting and drying practices, all of which may alter redox conditions and microbial processes governing CH~4~ and N~2~O fluxes. Moreover, mid-season drainage—a common practice for tillering control in high-yield systems—creates an aerobic-anaerobic transition that could trigger N~2~O pulses while suppressing CH~4~ production. To date, the trade-offs between CH~4~ suppression and N~2~O stimulation in such systems, as well as their integrated climatic impacts, require further quantification. Therefore, the objectives of this study were to (i) quantify CH~4~ and N~2~O emissions across the rice growing season in a high-yielding field, (ii) identify key emission episodes and their driving factors, and (iii) evaluate the global warming potential and emission intensity in relation to grain yield. The results are expected to inform management strategies that reconcile high productivity with climate change mitigation.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1. Site description and experimental design

A two-year field experiment (2022–2023) was conducted at the agricultural experimental station in Nanjing, Jiangsu Province, China (32°02′ N, 118°50′ E). The region has a subtropical monsoon climate with a mean annual temperature of 16.3 °C and annual precipitation of 1106 mm. The soil was a gleyic anthrosol (FAO classification) with a pH of 6.4, bulk density of 1.21 g cm⁻³, organic matter content of 27.8 g kg⁻¹, total nitrogen of 1.38 g kg⁻¹, and available phosphorus and potassium of 18.5 and 86.4 mg kg⁻¹, respectively. The rice cultivar used was Nangeng 9108, a high-yielding *japonica* super rice widely cultivated in the lower Yangtze River region. Seedlings were transplanted by hand on 20 June and harvested on 25 October in both years, with a hill spacing of 25 cm × 15 cm and three seedlings per hill.

2.2. Agronomic management

Nitrogen fertilizer was applied at a rate of 270 kg N ha⁻¹, split as 50% basal, 30% tillering, and 20% panicle initiation. Phosphorus (90 kg P~2~O~5~ ha⁻¹) and potassium (120 kg K~2~O ha⁻¹) were applied entirely as basal dressing. Water management followed local high-yield protocols: a 2–3 cm floodwater layer was maintained for the first two weeks after transplanting, followed by a 7-day mid-season drainage (MSD) at the maximum tillering stage. Subsequently, intermittent irrigation (alternating wetting and drying) was practiced until two weeks before harvest. Pesticides and herbicides were applied according to standard integrated pest management guidelines.

2.3. Greenhouse gas sampling and analysis

Fluxes of CH~4~ and N~2~O were measured using the static closed chamber method. Three replicate stainless-steel bases (50 cm × 50 cm × 15 cm) were permanently installed between rice hills in each plot. During sampling, a covered chamber (50 cm × 50 cm × 50 cm) equipped with a circulating fan and a thermometer was fitted onto the base. Gas samples were drawn from the headspace at 0 and 15 min using 50 mL polypropylene syringes. Sampling was performed between 09:00 and 11:00 h at 7-day intervals, with increased frequency (every 3 days) after fertilization, during MSD, and following heavy rainfall events. CH~4~ and N~2~O concentrations were determined within 24 h using a gas chromatograph equipped with a flame ionization detector (FID) and an electron capture detector (ECD). Gas fluxes were calculated from the linear change in concentration over time. Seasonal cumulative emissions were computed by linear interpolation between successive sampling dates. Global warming potential (GWP) was expressed as CO~2~ equivalents over a 100-year horizon using IPCC AR6 factors: 28 for CH~4~ and 265 for N~2~O. GHG emission intensity was calculated by dividing GWP by grain yield.

2.4. Statistical analysis

All statistical analyses were performed using SPSS 26.0. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was used to assess the effects of year and growth stage on gas fluxes. Means were compared using the least significant difference (LSD) test at *P* < 0.05. Pearson correlation analysis was applied to examine relationships between environmental factors and gas fluxes.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1. CH~4~ emission characteristics

CH~4~ fluxes exhibited pronounced seasonal variation with two distinct emission peaks across both years (Fig. 1). The first peak occurred during the active tillering stage (28–35 days after transplanting, DAT), reaching mean fluxes of 42.5 and 48.3 mg m⁻² h⁻¹ in 2022 and 2023, respectively. Following the mid-season drainage, CH~4~ emissions declined sharply to near-zero levels (< 1.0 mg m⁻² h⁻¹). Upon re-flooding, a second notable peak appeared during the booting stage (56–62 DAT), with fluxes averaging 38.6 and 44.1 mg m⁻² h⁻¹. Emissions gradually subsided after flowering. Seasonal cumulative CH~4~ emissions were 250.3 kg ha⁻¹ in 2022 and 278.4 kg ha⁻¹ in 2023. The higher emissions in 2023 were likely attributable to elevated mean temperatures (25.8 °C versus 24.3 °C in 2022) during the reproductive stage, which accelerated methanogenic activity.

3.2. N~2~O emission characteristics

N~2~O fluxes remained relatively low (< 50 μg m⁻² h⁻¹) during continuous flooding but increased markedly in response to water regime transitions. Notable pulse emissions were observed during the MSD period, with peak fluxes of 285.4 and 312.6 μg m⁻² h⁻¹ in 2022 and 2023, respectively. Smaller peaks coincided with top-dressing applications, particularly the panicle fertilizer under intermittently flooded conditions. Seasonal cumulative N~2~O emissions were 2.5 kg ha⁻¹ in 2022 and 3.1 kg ha⁻¹ in 2023. Although N~2~O pulses were transient, they contributed disproportionately to total seasonal N~2~O loss.

3.3. Yield, GWP, and emission intensity

Grain yields were 9.8 t ha⁻¹ in 2022 and 10.2 t ha⁻¹ in 2023. The corresponding GWPs were 7662.5 and 8605.5 kg CO~2~ eq ha⁻¹, with CH~4~ contributing approximately 91% and N~2~O contributing 9% to the total radiative forcing. GHG emission intensity was 0.78 kg CO~2~ eq kg⁻¹ grain in 2022 and 0.84 kg CO~2~ eq kg⁻¹ grain in 2023, with a two-year mean of 0.81 kg CO~2~ eq kg⁻¹ grain. Despite higher absolute GHG emissions in 2023, the concurrent increase in grain yield resulted in a marginal rise in emission intensity.

4. Discussion

The results demonstrate that high-yielding rice fields are substantial CH~4~ sources, with cumulative emissions exceeding those reported for conventional systems in the same agro-ecological zone. The bimodal emission pattern aligns with the developmental stages of maximum root exudation and labile carbon input, which fuel methanogenesis under anaerobic conditions. The mid-season drainage effectively disrupted methanogenic activity, as evidenced by the abrupt decline in CH~4~ fluxes; however, the subsequent re-introduction of oxygen stimulated nitrification-denitrification cycles, triggering N~2~O pulses. This antagonistic relationship between CH~4~ and N~2~O underscores the complexity of managing water regimes for net

title: CopulaNet: Learning residue co-evolution directly from multiple sequence alignment for protein structure prediction
text:
Protein structure prediction stands as a grand challenge in structural bioinformatics, with profound implications for understanding biological mechanisms and accelerating therapeutic design. A transformative advance in this field derives from the principle of residue co-evolution: physically interacting residues often display correlated mutation patterns across homologous sequences, thereby encoding spatial proximity within multiple sequence alignments (MSAs). Existing methods typically operationalize this principle through a two-stage pipeline, wherein handcrafted co-evolutionary statistics—such as covariance matrices or Markov random field potentials—are first extracted from MSAs and then processed by neural networks to predict contacts or distances. Nevertheless, this indirect strategy inevitably compresses the rich, high-order dependencies residing in the original sequence space into simplified statistical summaries, risking information loss and suboptimal feature representation.

To overcome this bottleneck, we introduce CopulaNet, an end-to-end deep learning architecture that learns residue co-evolution directly from raw MSAs, bypassing explicit feature extraction. Unlike conventional approaches that rely on pre-computed coupling matrices, CopulaNet operates on the original sequence space, preserving the full phylogenetic and covariation context of aligned sequences. By parameterizing residue dependencies through a deep neural formulation, the model automatically captures subtle co-evolutionary signatures often obscured by traditional statistical measures. This direct paradigm not only eliminates manual feature engineering but also establishes an uninterrupted information flow from sequence alignments to inter-residue geometric constraints. Extensive experiments demonstrate that CopulaNet delivers strong performance in protein structure prediction, underscoring the superiority of direct co-evolution learning over conventional multi-stage approaches.

title: Analysis of specialized nursing on respiratory functions in thoracotomy patients
text:
Results: On postoperative day 7, the specialized nursing group (n=52) exhibited superior respiratory function compared with controls (n=52). Mean FEV1 was 2.51±0.38 L versus 2.14±0.42 L (p<0.01), while FVC reached 3.28±0.46 L versus 2.82±0.53 L (p<0.05). Arterial blood gas analysis showed PaO2 of 90.1±6.0 mmHg versus 82.4±7.5 mmHg (p<0.01) and PaCO2 of 37.5±3.3 mmHg versus 43.6±4.8 mmHg (p<0.05). Peak expiratory flow was 271±44 L/min versus 234±49 L/min (p<0.05). Additionally, the intervention group demonstrated reduced pulmonary complications (9.6% vs 25.0%, p<0.05), fewer retained secretions (13.5% vs 30.8%, p<0.05), shorter chest tube duration (3.8±0.9 days vs 5.2±1.3 days, p<0.01), and decreased length of stay (9.4±1.6 days vs 11.7±2.2 days, p<0.01).

Discussion: These findings indicate that structured specialized nursing, including incentive spirometry guidance and targeted airway management, markedly improves post-thoracotomy pulmonary recovery. By enhancing mucus clearance and optimizing alveolar ventilation, this approach significantly reduces complications and accelerates clinical rehabilitation, supporting its routine integration into thoracic surgical care pathways.

title: Causes of vision loss at China's largest blind school during a period of significant economic growth: 2008-2016
text:
Causes of vision loss at China's largest blind school during a period of significant economic growth: 2008-2016

Abstract

Background: China experienced rapid economic growth and health-system reform between 2008 and 2016, which profoundly altered the epidemiology of childhood blindness. This study aimed to characterize the causes of severe vision loss among students enrolled at China’s largest residential blind school during this transformative period.

Methods: A retrospective chart review was conducted for all students admitted between January 2008 and December 2016. Demographic data, comprehensive ophthalmic examination records, and etiological classifications were extracted. Causes of vision loss were categorized as congenital/hereditary, perinatal (including retinopathy of prematurity), infectious/inflammatory, traumatic, and other acquired conditions. Trends were analyzed across three time strata (2008–2010, 2011–2013, and 2014–2016).

Results: Of the 712 students identified, 438 (61.5%) were male and 274 (38.5%) were female, with a mean age at admission of 8.4 ± 2.1 years. Overall, congenital and hereditary disorders accounted for 56.2% (n = 400) of cases, followed by perinatal factors at 12.1% (n = 86), infectious or inflammatory conditions at 11.4% (n = 81), trauma at 7.6% (n = 54), and other acquired causes at 12.7% (n = 91). Over the study period, the proportion of congenital/hereditary causes rose from 48.3% in 2008–2010 to 63.8% in 2014–2016 (p < 0.01), while infectious/inflammatory etiologies declined from 17.2% to 6.9% (p < 0.01). Notably, retinopathy of prematurity increased from 2.1% to 8.6% (p = 0.02). Students from rural areas constituted 64.6% of the cohort, yet this proportion decreased significantly over time.

Conclusion: The etiological profile of blindness in this cohort shifted markedly toward congenital and hereditary conditions and perinatal complications, reflecting improved control of infectious eye diseases but highlighting persistent gaps in neonatal screening and genetic counseling. These findings underscore the need for targeted public health strategies aligned with China’s evolving demographic and healthcare landscape.

Keywords: childhood blindness, etiology, retinopathy of prematurity, congenital cataract, China, epidemiology

1. Introduction

Blindness in children represents a profound public health challenge, carrying lifelong implications for education, employment, and social integration. The World Health Organization estimates that 1.4 million children worldwide are irreversibly blind, with approximately 75% of cases concentrated in Asia and Africa. The etiology of childhood vision loss is closely tied to socioeconomic development; while low-income regions bear a disproportionate burden of preventable infectious and nutritional eye diseases, affluent nations predominantly report genetic, congenital, and perinatal causes.

China, the world’s most populous nation, underwent extraordinary economic expansion between 2008 and 2016, with per capita GDP nearly doubling and healthcare expenditure growing substantially. During this period, the government expanded the New Rural Cooperative Medical Scheme and launched national programs targeting preventable blindness, including childhood cataract initiatives. These developments likely altered the relative contribution of infectious, traumatic, and congenital factors to pediatric vision impairment. However, data from specialized education institutions—which capture the most severe cases of childhood blindness—remain scarce. Residential blind schools in China serve children with bilateral severe visual impairment or blindness who require adapted curricula, making them valuable sentinel sites for monitoring secular trends in etiology.

The objective of this study was to delineate the causes of vision loss among students admitted to China’s largest blind school between 2008 and 2016. By analyzing nearly a decade of data encompassing a period of sweeping socioeconomic transition, we sought to identify shifting patterns in blindness etiology and inform evidence-based policy for pediatric eye care and special education resource allocation.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study design and setting

This retrospective cohort study was conducted at the largest government-funded residential blind school in China, located in eastern China and currently serving approximately 600 students from preschool through high school. The institution admits students from across the nation based on bilateral severe visual impairment (best-corrected visual acuity < 20/400 in the better eye) or profound visual field restriction.

2.2 Participants and data collection

All consecutive students admitted between January 1, 2008, and December 31, 2016, were eligible for inclusion. Demographic variables (sex, age at admission, and rural/urban household registration status) were extracted from admission registers. Ophthalmic data were retrieved from standardized clinical records compiled during mandatory pre-admission evaluations, which included visual acuity assessment, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, dilated fundus examination, B-scan ultrasonography when media opacities precluded a retinal view, and electrophysiological testing when indicated. For students admitted without prior documentation, examinations were completed by a tertiary hospital ophthalmology service affiliated with the school.

2.3 Etiological classification

The primary cause of vision loss was classified according to the modified World Health Organization Prevention of Blindness and Deafness coding criteria by a senior pediatric ophthalmologist (L.Z.). Categories comprised: (1) congenital/hereditary (e.g., microphthalmos, anophthalmos, congenital cataract, congenital glaucoma, retinal dystrophies, optic nerve hypoplasia); (2) perinatal (e.g., retinopathy of prematurity [ROP], perinatal hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy with cortical visual impairment); (3) infectious/inflammatory (e.g., corneal scarring secondary to vitamin A deficiency, keratomalacia, endophthalmitis, or trachoma); (4) traumatic; and (5) other acquired (e.g., tumors, glaucoma, uncorrected aphakia). When multiple pathologies coexisted, the principal insult most directly responsible for the presenting visual disability was designated as the primary cause.

2.4 Statistical analysis

Data were analyzed using SPSS version 22.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Descriptive statistics were expressed as frequencies, percentages, and means with standard deviations. The Cochran-Armitage trend test was used to assess temporal trends in categorical variables across the three time strata. Pearson’s chi-square test compared proportions between demographic subgroups. A two-tailed p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The study protocol was approved by the institutional ethics committee, and waiver of informed consent was granted given the retrospective design and use of de-identified data.

3. Results and Analysis

A total of 712 students were enrolled during the nine-year period. The cohort was predominantly male (61.5%, n = 438), reflecting the well-documented male predominance in several congenital eye disorders. The mean age at admission was 8.4 ± 2.1 years, with no significant temporal variation. Rural household registration was recorded for 460 students (64.6%); however, the rural proportion declined from 71.4% in 2008–2010 to 58.3% in 2014–2016 (p = 0.003).

3.1 Overall etiological distribution

Congenital and hereditary disorders constituted the largest category, affecting 400 students (56.2%). Within this group, microphthalmos/anophthalmos/coloboma accounted for 22.8% (n = 91) of congenital cases, inherited retinal dystrophies for 20.0% (n = 80), congenital cataract for 18.5% (n = 74), optic nerve hypoplasia for 15.5% (n = 62), and congenital glaucoma for 12.0% (n = 48). Perinatal causes were identified in 86 students (12.1%), of whom 41 (5.8% of total) had ROP and 45 (6.3%) had cortical or optic pathway injuries attributable to perinatal hypoxia. Infectious or inflammatory etiologies were responsible for 81 cases (11.4%), most commonly corneal opacification from previous keratitis or vitamin A deficiency. Trauma caused unilateral or bilateral blindness in 54 students (7.6%), while miscellaneous acquired conditions accounted for 91 cases (12.7%).

3.2 Temporal trends

Marked shifts in etiology were observed over the three time strata (Table 1). The proportion of congenital/hereditary causes increased steadily from 48.3% (82/170) in 2008–2010 to 56.1% (131/233) in 2011–2013, and further to 63.8% (187/293) in 2014–2016 (Z = 3.42, p < 0.001). Conversely, infectious/inflammatory causes declined sharply from 17.2% (29/170) to 10.3% (24/233) and 6.9% (20/293) (Z = -3.89, p < 0.001). Traumatic vision loss also decreased from 9.4% to 6.9% and 6.5%, though the trend did not reach statistical significance (Z = -1.42, p = 0.16).

The most striking temporal change occurred within perinatal etiologies. While overall perinatal causes remained relatively stable at 11.8%, 12.0%, and 12.3% across the three strata, the contribution of ROP rose significantly from 2.1% (n = 3) in 2008–2010 to 5.2% (n = 12) in 2011–2013, and to 8.6% (n = 25) in 2014–2016 (Z = 3.11, p = 0.002). Meanwhile, the proportion of cortical visual impairment from perinatal hypoxia remained constant.

3.3 Rural versus urban disparities

Students from rural backgrounds demonstrated a significantly higher prevalence of infectious/inflammatory causes compared with their urban counterparts (14.3% vs. 6.3%, p < 0.001) and traumatic etiologies (9.3% vs. 4.4%, p = 0.01). Conversely, ROP was more prevalent among urban registrants (7.4% vs. 4.3%, p = 0.04), likely reflecting higher rates of preterm birth survival in urban tertiary neonatal centers. No significant rural-urban difference was observed for congenital/hereditary causes (55.4% vs. 57.9%, p = 0.52).

4. Discussion

This large retrospective study reveals a decisive epidemiological transition in the causes of severe childhood vision loss at China’s largest blind school between 2008 and 2016. The data document a declining burden of infectious and inflammatory eye diseases alongside a rising predominance of congenital, hereditary, and perinatal conditions, particularly ROP. These trends mirror China’s rapid socioeconomic advancement and concurrent health-system strengthening, yet they also expose emerging challenges in pediatric ophthalmology.

The decline in infectious and inflammatory blindness—from 17.2% to 6.9%—likely reflects the cumulative impact of public health interventions, including the nationwide vitamin A supplementation program, improved measles immunization coverage, and enhanced access to primary eye care in rural areas. This trajectory aligns with patterns observed in other middle-income countries undergoing economic development. Nevertheless, the persistent rural excess in infectious and traumatic causes indicates that geographic and socioeconomic inequities in eye care access have not been fully eliminated.

The ascending proportion of congenital and hereditary disorders, which approached two-thirds of all cases by 2014–2016, is consistent with reports from high-income East Asian regions. As infant mortality declines and control of acquired infections improves, genetic conditions assume greater relative importance. This shift carries significant implications for service planning. Blind schools must increasingly accommodate students with complex multisystem syndromes and low vision rehabilitation needs, while clinical services should expand access to genetic counseling and molecular diagnostic capabilities.

The doubling of ROP prevalence over the study period is particularly noteworthy. Expanded neonatal intensive care capacity during China’s economic boom markedly improved survival among very-low-birth-weight infants; however, retinal screening programs have lagged behind, especially in secondary-level hospitals. The urban concentration of ROP observed in our cohort supports this interpretation, as advanced neonatal care is concentrated in major cities. Without systematic implementation of international ROP screening guidelines, China risks facing an iatrogenic epidemic of preventable childhood blindness—a pattern already documented in other emerging economies.

Several limitations warrant consideration. First, as a single-center study based at a specialized school, our findings may not generalize to children with moderate visual impairment integrated into mainstream schools or to those unable to access special education. Second, etiological classification relied on retrospective clinical records; subtle diagnostic shifts over time could not be entirely excluded. Third, the study captures only students with bilateral severe vision loss, potentially underestimating unilateral traumatic or infectious causes. Finally, genetic confirmation was unavailable for most hereditary cases, precluding precise molecular subtyping.

5. Conclusion

Between 2008 and 2016, the etiological landscape of severe childhood vision loss at China’s largest blind school underwent substantial transformation. While the decline in infection-related and traumatic blindness signals progress in public health and primary care, the escalating burden of congenital, hereditary, and perinatal causes—especially ROP—demands urgent policy attention. Future strategies should prioritize universal ROP screening for at-risk neonates, expansion of genetic counseling services, and continued reduction of rural-urban disparities in eye care access. Blind schools, as repositories of the most affected children, offer invaluable sentinel data for tracking these evolving trends and evaluating the population-level impact of pediatric eye health interventions in an era of rapid economic change.

title: Dynamic assessment of urban economy-environment-energy system using system dynamics model: A case study in Beijing
text:
Dynamic assessment of urban economy-environment-energy system using system dynamics model: A case study in Beijing

---

Abstract

Urban economy-environment-energy (3E) systems are characterized by complex feedbacks that challenge conventional static assessments. This study develops a system dynamics (SD) model to dynamically evaluate the 3E nexus in Beijing, China, covering 2010–2030. The model integrates economic growth, energy consumption structure, and environmental emissions through five interacting subsystems and twenty-eight causal feedback loops. Historical data from 2010–2019 were used for calibration, and three scenarios—Business as Usual (BAU), Green Development (GD), and Industrial Restructuring (IR)—were simulated to 2030. Results indicate that under BAU, Beijing’s CO₂ emissions continue rising to 193.4 Mt by 2030, whereas the GD scenario drives an emissions peak in 2028 at 165.2 Mt alongside a 35.2% reduction in energy intensity. The IR scenario yields a moderate trajectory, balancing economic expansion with a 2029 emissions peak. The findings highlight that coordinated clean-energy subsidies and tertiary-sector upgrading are critical for achieving urban sustainability. The proposed SD framework offers a replicable approach for dynamic 3E management in megacities.

Keywords: System dynamics; Economy-environment-energy nexus; Urban sustainability; Beijing; Scenario analysis; Carbon emissions peak

---

1. Introduction

Rapid urbanization has intensified the interdependencies among economic development, energy consumption, and environmental degradation, forming a complex “3E” system. Megacities such as Beijing face acute tensions: they must sustain economic vitality while confronting rigid energy constraints and stringent air-quality targets. Traditional econometric models often fail to capture the feedbacks and delays inherent in these systems, leading to policy prescriptions that overlook long-term trade-offs. System dynamics (SD), pioneered by Forrester, offers a simulation-based approach to model nonlinear interactions, stock-flow structures, and time lags, making it particularly suited for urban sustainability research.

Beijing exemplifies these challenges. Over the past decade, the city has shuttered heavy industry and expanded its service economy, yet it remains reliant on imported electricity and fossil fuels, and its ambient PM₂.₅ levels periodically exceed health guidelines. While previous studies have examined Beijing’s carbon footprint or energy efficiency in isolation, integrated dynamic assessments of the 3E nexus remain scarce. To bridge this gap, this study constructs an SD model tailored to Beijing’s socio-economic context. The objectives are threefold: (1) to map the causal mechanisms linking economic output, energy mix, and pollutant emissions; (2) to validate the model against historical trends; and (3) to project future trajectories under alternative policy scenarios. The findings are intended to inform evidence-based strategies for synergistic urban governance.

---

2. Materials and Methods

The SD model boundary encompasses Beijing’s administrative area with a simulation horizon of 2010–2030 and a one-year time step. The model comprises five subsystems: Economic Production, Population & Employment, Energy Consumption, Environmental Emissions, and Policy Intervention. Causal loop diagrams were developed through stakeholder consultation and literature review, revealing twenty-eight feedback loops. Key positive loops include “economic growth → energy demand → fossil fuel combustion → emissions,” while negative loops capture “environmental damage → remediation cost → capital diversion” and “carbon tax → clean energy investment → emission reduction.”

Stock-and-flow structures were built in Vensim® DSS. Major state variables include GDP, permanent population, total energy consumption, CO₂ stock, and PM₂.₅ concentration. Auxiliary variables represent energy intensity, tertiary industry share, coal-to-gas ratio, and desulfurization efficiency. Model equations take the form of integral difference equations; for example, GDP(*t*) = GDP(*t*−d*t*) + d*t* × (investment return − depreciation − environmental penalty), parameterized using elasticity coefficients derived from historical regression. Invented but realistic baseline data were constructed to reflect Beijing’s profile: GDP was set at 1.41 trillion CNY in 2010, rising to 3.54 trillion CNY in 2019; total energy consumption increased from 69.5 Mtce to 73.8 Mtce; and annual CO₂ emissions grew from 122.3 Mt to 148.6 Mt over the same period.

Three scenarios were designed. Business as Usual (BAU) extrapolates current trends without new policies. Green Development (GD) imposes a carbon tax of 80 CNY/t CO₂, raises the annual clean-energy subsidy by 12%, and caps coal consumption at 8.0 Mtce by 2030. Industrial Restructuring (IR) accelerates the tertiary sector share from 83.5% (2019) to 87.0% by 2030 while phasing out high-energy manufacturing. Model validity was assessed through historical fit tests (Mean Absolute Percentage Error, MAPE < 8%) and extreme-condition sensitivity analysis.

---

3. Results

The calibrated model closely reproduced historical trends for 2010–2019, with MAPE values of 3.2% for GDP, 4.1% for energy consumption, and 5.8% for CO₂ emissions, confirming structural reliability. Under BAU, Beijing’s GDP is projected to reach 6.82 trillion CNY by 2030, accompanied by energy consumption of 88.4 Mtce and CO₂ emissions of 193.4 Mt. PM₂.₅ annual average concentration declines only marginally to 37.8 μg/m³ because transport and building-sector emissions persist.

In the GD scenario, aggressive decarbonization policies reduce energy intensity by 35.2% relative to 2010. Total energy demand peaks at 77.1 Mtce in 2028 before falling to 75.3 Mtce by 2030, with the clean-energy share rising to 34.8%. CO₂ emissions peak in 2028 at 165.2 Mt and decline to 161.5 Mt by 2030. The carbon tax temporarily dampens GDP growth, yielding 6.34 trillion CNY in 2030—7.0% lower than BAU—but PM₂.₅ drops to 27.4 μg/m³.

The IR scenario produces intermediate outcomes. Structural upgrading restrains energy demand to 79.6 Mtce by 2030, and CO₂ emissions peak in 2029 at 174.8 Mt. GDP reaches 6.51 trillion CNY in 2030, as the shift to services lowers industrial emissions faster than transport emissions rise. Notably, the interaction between industrial structure and energy mix generates a synergistic effect: the combined GD+IR hybrid scenario (tested sensitivity-wise) projects a 2027 emissions peak at 158.3 Mt, suggesting policy complementarity.

---

4. Discussion

The simulation results underscore that Beijing’s 3E system is governed by competing feedback loops where short-term economic costs can secure long-term environmental dividends. The two-year advancement of the emissions peak under the GD scenario (2028 versus 2030 under BAU) demonstrates that pricing mechanisms and clean-energy subsidies can overcome inertia in the fossil-fuel-dependent building and transport sectors. However, the model also reveals a “rebound-like” effect under BAU: rising incomes drive greater per-capita electricity consumption in the services sector, partially offsetting efficiency gains. This aligns with broader observations in post-industrial megacities where tertiary-sector electrification outpaces decarbonization of the power mix.

Industrial restructuring alone (IR) offers a smoother economic transition but delays the emissions peak because service-sector growth stimulates mobility demand. Consequently, no single lever is sufficient; the super-additive outcome of the GD+IR hybrid indicates that structural and technological policies must be synchronized. A limitation of this study is the assumption of exogenous technological progress; endogenous innovation loops could be incorporated in future work. Moreover, cross-boundary electricity emissions are treated as a fixed import factor, whereas a spatially explicit model could better capture Beijing’s reliance on transferred emissions.

---

5. Conclusion

This study developed a system dynamics model to dynamically assess Beijing’s urban economy-environment-energy system. The validated model reveals that under conventional development pathways, Beijing’s CO₂ emissions will continue rising through 2030. By contrast, integrated Green Development and Industrial Restructuring policies can advance the emissions peak to 2027–2028 while maintaining moderate economic growth. Policymakers are advised to combine carbon pricing with tertiary-sector upgrading and clean-energy infrastructure investment to exploit synergies within the 3E nexus. The SD framework presented here is adaptable to other megacities seeking to navigate the trade-offs between prosperity, energy security, and environmental quality.

title: Relationship between FDI, fiscal expenditure and green total-factor productivity in China: From the perspective of spatial spillover
text: This study investigates the nexus between foreign direct investment (FDI), fiscal expenditure, and green total-factor productivity (GTFP) in China from a spatial spillover perspective. Utilizing provincial panel data spanning 2000–2020, a spatial Durbin model is employed to empirically decompose total effects into direct and indirect spillover components. The results reveal that both FDI and fiscal expenditure significantly promote local GTFP. Importantly, these factors also generate positive spatial spillover effects on GTFP in neighboring regions, indicating that cross-regional capital flows and public spending yield transboundary green growth externalities. Furthermore, marked regional heterogeneity is identified, with the promoting effects being substantially more pronounced in eastern China than in central and western areas. These findings imply that optimizing FDI structures, improving fiscal expenditure efficiency, and strengthening inter-regional policy coordination are critical for advancing sustainable high-quality development and achieving coordinated green transformation nationwide.

title: MicroRNA repertoire for functional genome research in tilapia identified by deep sequencing
text:
MicroRNA repertoire for functional genome research in tilapia identified by deep sequencing

Abstract

MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are small non-coding RNAs that serve as pivotal post-transcriptional regulators in eukaryotes. Despite the agricultural significance of Nile tilapia (*Oreochromis niloticus*), its microRNAome remains largely unexplored, limiting functional genomic studies. In this study, we employed high-throughput Illumina sequencing to systematically characterize small RNA populations in the liver, brain, and skeletal muscle of adult tilapia. After filtering, approximately 24.6 million clean reads were generated, yielding 387 conserved miRNAs and 62 candidate novel miRNAs. Comparative profiling identified 89 differentially expressed miRNAs across tissues, with distinct tissue-enriched signatures reflecting specialized physiological functions. Bioinformatic prediction uncovered 14,256 putative target genes significantly enriched in pathways related to metabolism, signal transduction, and development. Stem-loop quantitative real-time PCR confirmed the sequencing-derived expression patterns (Pearson’s *r* = 0.91, *P* < 0.01). This comprehensive miRNA atlas provides an essential foundation for dissecting gene regulatory networks and supports future functional genome research and selective breeding in tilapia.

Keywords: miRNA; Nile tilapia; deep sequencing; functional genomics; target prediction; aquaculture

1. Introduction

Nile tilapia (*Oreochromis niloticus*) ranks among the most economically important freshwater aquaculture species worldwide, with annual production exceeding six million metric tons. As a model cichlid, it also offers unique insights into vertebrate evolution, sex determination, and adaptive radiation. Deciphering the molecular mechanisms that govern growth performance, disease resistance, and environmental adaptation is therefore critical for both basic biology and aquaculture improvement. MicroRNAs (miRNAs), a class of endogenous ~22-nucleotide non-coding RNAs, mediate post-transcriptional gene silencing primarily through imperfect base-pairing with the 3′ untranslated regions of target messenger RNAs. By fine-tuning protein output, miRNAs influence virtually every biological process, including cell differentiation, energy metabolism, apoptosis, and immune defense.

While the chromosomal-level tilapia genome assembly has accelerated gene discovery, annotation of its non-coding regulatory landscape remains incomplete. To date, only a handful of miRNAs have been experimentally validated in tilapia, and most studies have relied on homology-based predictions that miss lineage-specific or low-abundance species. High-throughput sequencing circumvents these limitations by enabling *de novo* identification of small RNAs without prior sequence knowledge. Here, we constructed small RNA libraries from liver, brain, and muscle—three tissues central to growth, metabolism, and neural control—and subjected them to Illumina deep sequencing. Our objectives were to (i) expand the catalog of tilapia miRNAs, (ii) profile tissue-specific expression patterns, and (iii) predict downstream regulatory networks. The resulting dataset provides a robust platform for functional genome research and molecular-assisted breeding.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Sample collection and RNA extraction. Healthy adult Nile tilapia (*n* = 6, mixed sex, body weight 450 ± 30 g) were reared in freshwater recirculating tanks at 28 ± 1 °C. After anesthesia, liver, brain, and skeletal muscle tissues were rapidly dissected, flash-frozen in liquid nitrogen, and stored at −80 °C. Total RNA was isolated using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA purity and integrity were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (A260/A280 > 1.9) and an Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 (RIN > 8.0), respectively.

2.2 Small RNA library construction and sequencing. Equal quantities of total RNA from two individuals were pooled per tissue to create three biological replicate libraries. Small RNAs of 18–30 nt were size-fractionated by 15% denaturing polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis, ligated to proprietary 5′ and 3′ RNA adapters, reverse-transcribed, and amplified by 12 cycles of PCR. The purified cDNA libraries were quantified with a Qubit 2.0 fluorometer and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq 2500 platform, generating 50-bp single-end reads.

2.3 Bioinformatic analysis. Raw reads were trimmed to remove adapter sequences, low-quality bases (Phred score < 20), reads shorter than 18 nt, and contaminants. Unique clean reads were aligned to the *O. niloticus* reference genome (GenBank: GCF_001858045.2) using Bowtie v1.2.3, allowing one mismatch. Known miRNAs were annotated by mapping against miRBase 22.0. Novel miRNA precursors were predicted using miRDeep2, with strict criteria requiring characteristic stem-loop folding and Dicer cleavage signatures. Read counts were normalized to transcripts per million (TPM). Differential expression across tissues was analyzed with DESeq2, employing a threshold of |log2 fold change| ≥ 1 and adjusted *P*-value < 0.05 (Benjamini–Hochberg correction). Putative target genes were predicted using TargetFish (integrating TargetScan and miRanda algorithms) and subjected to Gene Ontology (GO) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) enrichment analyses using DAVID v6.8. Selected miRNAs were validated by stem-loop qRT-PCR with U6 snRNA as the endogenous control.

3. Results and Analysis

3.1 Overview of sequencing data. Sequencing of the nine libraries generated 26.8 million raw reads. After quality control, 24.6 million clean reads remained, of which 82.4% successfully mapped to the tilapia genome. Length distribution analysis revealed a prominent peak at 22 nucleotides, consistent with mature miRNA biogenesis, and a nucleotide bias toward uracil at the 5′ end (67.3%). Annotation of small RNA categories indicated that miRNAs accounted for 48.6% of total reads, followed by unannotated small RNAs (28.1%), transfer RNAs (12.4%), ribosomal RNAs (7.3%), and small nuclear/nucleolar RNAs (3.6%).

3.2 Identification of conserved and novel miRNAs. We identified 387 conserved miRNAs distributed across 124 families. Ubiquitous families included let-7, miR-10, miR-26, and miR-30. Notably, 62 candidate novel miRNAs were discovered, each supported by stable precursor hairpin structures with minimum free energies ranging from −32.4 to −18.7 kcal/mol and mature star sequences detected for 58 of them.

3.3 Tissue-specific expression profiles. Pairwise comparisons identified 89 differentially expressed miRNAs (DEMs) across the three tissues. Muscle exhibited 32 tissue-specific DEMs, including highly abundant miR-1, miR-133a, and miR-206, collectively known as myomiRs. The liver was enriched for 28 DEMs, notably miR-122 (TPM = 18,420) and miR-192, implicated in lipid and glucose homeostasis. The brain displayed 29 DEMs, with miR-9, miR-124, and miR-128 showing the highest enrichment, consistent with neuronal differentiation and synaptic plasticity.

3.4 Target prediction and functional annotation. A total of 14,256 protein-coding genes were predicted as putative targets of the identified miRNAs. GO enrichment analysis revealed significant overrepresentation in biological processes such as signal transduction (*P* = 2.4 × 10⁻¹²), transcriptional regulation (*P* = 8.7 × 10⁻¹⁰), metabolic processes (*P* = 5.1 × 10⁻⁹), and immune response (*P* = 3.3 × 10⁻⁶). KEGG pathway analysis highlighted the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway, MAPK cascade, fatty acid degradation, and AMPK signaling as significantly enriched (adjusted *P* < 0.01). Intriguingly, liver-specific miRNA targets were strongly associated with insulin resistance and glycerolipid metabolism pathways, suggesting a central role for miRNAs in hepatic energy partitioning.

3.5 qRT-PCR validation. Eight miRNAs spanning a wide expression range were selected for stem-loop qRT-PCR, including four conserved and four novel candidates. Expression trends were concordant with deep sequencing data, yielding a Pearson correlation coefficient of 0.91 (*P* < 0.01), thereby confirming the reliability of our sequencing and bioinformatic pipeline.

4. Discussion

This study establishes the most comprehensive tissue-resolved miRNA atlas for Nile tilapia to date. The identification of 387 conserved and 62 novel miRNAs substantially expands the known regulatory repertoire and corrects the previous reliance on cross-species homology predictions. The canonical 22-nt length distribution, 5′ uracil bias, and stable precursor folding energies all conform to the defining features of vertebrate miRNAs, supporting the high fidelity of our annotation pipeline.

The observed tissue-specific expression patterns align closely with those documented in zebrafish, medaka, and mammals, underscoring deep evolutionary conservation of miRNA-mediated regulation. The dominance of myomiRs in skeletal muscle and miR-122 in liver suggests that these regulatory circuits were already established in the teleost ancestor and have been maintained under strong purifying selection. From an aquaculture perspective, the enrichment of AMPK and fatty acid metabolism pathways among hepatic miRNA targets is particularly significant. Manipulating miR-122 or miR-192 levels could potentially modulate lipid deposition and fillet quality, traits of major economic interest. Similarly, the brain-enriched miR-9 and miR-124 may regulate neuroendocrine axes influencing feeding behavior and stress responses.

The 62 novel miRNAs, absent from miRBase and previous fish surveys, likely include tilapia-specific or cichlid-family regulators. Their generally lower abundance compared with conserved miRNAs is consistent with the evolutionary model that young miRNAs emerge at low expression levels and acquire targets gradually. Whether these novel molecules contribute to lineage-specific traits—such as the remarkable dietary plasticity of tilapia—warrants further investigation. Limitations include the restricted tissue panel and absence of experimental challenges (e.g., bacterial infection or hypoxia). Future work should integrate multi-condition sequencing and experimental validation through dual-luciferase reporter assays or CRISPR-based knockout to construct a dynamic, systems-level view of tilapia gene regulation.

5. Conclusion

Through Illumina deep sequencing of liver, brain, and muscle tissues, we identified 449 miRNAs in Nile tilapia, comprising 387 conserved and 62 novel species. Tissue-specific expression profiling revealed distinct regulatory signatures linked to myogenesis, hepatic metabolism, and neural function. Target prediction and pathway enrichment further highlighted roles in growth, energy homeostasis, and signal transduction. The validated dataset reported here provides an essential genomic resource for functional studies in tilapia and related teleosts. It lays the groundwork for deciphering miRNA-guided gene networks and may facilitate the development of molecular markers to accelerate genetic improvement in tilapia aquaculture.

title: Changes of cell wall components during embryogenesis of Castanea mollissima
text: Embryogenesis is a pivotal process governing the transition from zygotes to mature embryos, fundamentally determining seed quality and plant propagation. In woody species, this process involves complex developmental programs. Castanea mollissima, an economically important nut tree native to China, represents a valuable model for studying embryonic development in hardwoods. The plant cell wall, a dynamic extracellular matrix, critically regulates cell division, elongation, and differentiation during embryogenesis by providing mechanical support and mediating cell-cell communication. Although cell wall biology has been extensively studied in herbaceous models, the spatiotemporal dynamics of cell wall components—such as pectin, hemicellulose, and cellulose—during embryogenesis remain poorly understood in C. mollissima. Characterizing these compositional changes is essential for elucidating the molecular mechanisms underlying embryo pattern formation and cell fate specification. This study aimed to systematically investigate the variations in cell wall components throughout embryogenesis in C. mollissima, thereby providing insights into the developmental regulation of woody plant embryogenesis.

title: Loss accounting of environmental pollution within Pearl River Delta region, South China
text:
The integrated loss-accounting framework estimated that environmental pollution across the Pearl River Delta (PRD) imposed an annual economic loss of approximately 156.8 billion RMB (USD 22.1 billion) in 2022, equivalent to 3.2% of the region’s GDP. Air pollution constituted the single largest component, accounting for 70.5 billion RMB (45.0% of total losses), driven mainly by PM2.5 and surface ozone-related health costs, absenteeism, and premature mortality. Water pollution ranked second at 50.2 billion RMB (32.0%), stemming from eutrophication in the Pearl River Estuary, diminished fisheries, and groundwater contamination beneath the Dongguan–Foshan manufacturing corridor. Soil degradation and hazardous solid-waste accumulation contributed 23.5 billion RMB (15.0%), while loss of wetland and forest ecosystem services represented 12.6 billion RMB (8.0%). Sectorally, manufacturing dominated at 86.2 billion RMB (55%), followed by agriculture at 31.4 billion RMB (20%) and urban services at 39.2 billion RMB (25%). Spatially, losses concentrated in Dongguan (18.7 billion RMB), Foshan (16.3 billion RMB), and Guangzhou (21.4 billion RMB), whereas Shenzhen’s cleaner service economy limited its share to 12.1 billion RMB. Per capita loss averaged 2,840 RMB region-wide.

These findings indicate that unpriced pollution externalities erode a substantial share of the PRD’s economic output. The 3.2% GDP loss is comparable to estimates for other major industrialized deltas in East Asia but exceeds the 2.1% recorded for the Yangtze River Delta, underscoring the environmental cost of the PRD’s export-oriented, energy-intensive manufacturing base. Our accounting likely represents a conservative lower bound because non-market ecosystem services, long-term carcinogenic effects, and biodiversity irreversibility were not fully monetized. Sensitivity analysis showed that varying the value of statistical life by ±20% altered total losses by 11.4 billion RMB, confirming health damages as the dominant uncertainty source. Spatially, the concentration of losses in Dongguan, Foshan, and the western bank of the Pearl River suggests that targeted industrial upgrading, stricter cross-boundary emission standards, and Guangdong–Hong Kong–Macau ecological compensation funds could yield disproportionate economic benefits. Ultimately, reframing pollution abatement as a safeguard of net regional productivity, rather than a mere regulatory burden, is essential for sustainable growth in South China.

title: The role of three-dimensional printed models of skull in anatomy education: a randomized controlled trail
text:
The role of three-dimensional printed models of skull in anatomy education: a randomized controlled trial

Abstract

Background: Three-dimensional (3D) printing technology has emerged as an innovative tool in medical education, yet its efficacy compared with traditional methods in skull anatomy teaching remains insufficiently validated through rigorous randomized trials. Objective: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) aimed to evaluate the effectiveness of 3D-printed skull models versus conventional two-dimensional (2D) didactic resources in improving anatomical knowledge, spatial understanding, and student satisfaction among medical undergraduates. Methods: A total of 96 first-year medical students were randomly allocated to either the 3D-printed model group (*n* = 48) or the control group (*n* = 48) utilizing textbooks and digital 2D images. Over a two-week intervention period, both groups underwent standardized skull anatomy instruction. Outcomes included pre- and post-intervention theoretical examination scores, a practical structure-identification test, the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test–Rotations (PSVT-R), and a validated satisfaction questionnaire. Results: Post-intervention, the 3D-printed model group demonstrated significantly greater improvement in theoretical scores (mean difference 14.2 vs. 9.8; *p* < 0.001) and practical identification accuracy (87.3% vs. 72.6%; *p* < 0.001) compared with controls. Spatial visualization ability improved significantly in the intervention group (ΔPSVT-R: 5.4 ± 3.1 vs. 2.1 ± 2.8; *p* < 0.001). Student satisfaction was also significantly higher in the 3D model group (4.6 ± 0.5 vs. 3.7 ± 0.7; *p* < 0.001). Conclusion: Integrating 3D-printed skull models into anatomy education significantly enhances learning outcomes, spatial reasoning, and student satisfaction compared with traditional 2D methods. These findings support the adoption of 3D printing technology as a valuable adjunct in undergraduate neuroanatomy and cranial osteology curricula.

Keywords: Three-dimensional printing; Skull anatomy; Medical education; Randomized controlled trial; Spatial visualization; Anatomy teaching

1. Introduction

Anatomy remains a cornerstone of medical education, providing the foundational spatial and structural knowledge essential for clinical practice. However, contemporary anatomy teaching faces mounting challenges, including declining cadaveric dissection opportunities, ethical concerns regarding specimen procurement, and the cognitive burden associated with translating two-dimensional (2D) representations into three-dimensional (3D) mental models. The human skull, with its intricate foramina, sutures, and asymmetrical pneumatic cavities, represents one of the most cognitively demanding regions for novice learners. Traditional pedagogical approaches relying on textbooks, atlases, and digital images often fail to convey the complex topographic relationships inherent to cranial anatomy, potentially impeding the development of accurate spatial reasoning.

In recent years, 3D printing technology has garnered substantial attention as an innovative educational adjunct. By converting computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) datasets into tangible, patient-specific models, 3D printing offers haptic feedback and allows unrestricted physical manipulation, theoretically bridging the gap between 2D imagery and cadaveric specimens. Preliminary observational studies suggest that 3D-printed anatomical models may improve student engagement and comprehension. Nevertheless, the literature lacks robust, randomized controlled evidence quantifying the educational value of 3D-printed skull models relative to standard resources. To address this evidence gap, we conducted a randomized controlled trial to determine whether the integration of 3D-printed skull models into a structured anatomy module improves learning outcomes, spatial visualization skills, and perceived educational satisfaction among first-year medical students compared with conventional 2D-based instruction.

2. Materials and Methods

2.1 Study Design and Participants

This single-center, parallel-group, randomized controlled trial was conducted at the Anatomy Department of [Fictional University] between September and November 2024. First-year medical students enrolled in the gross anatomy course were invited to participate. Inclusion criteria required participants to be first-year medical students with no prior formal university-level anatomy training. Students with prior degrees in anatomy or extensive experience with 3D anatomical software were excluded. Using a computer-generated randomization sequence with block sizes of four, eligible participants were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio) to either the intervention group (3D-printed skull model instruction) or the control group (traditional 2D instruction). Group allocation was concealed in sequentially numbered, opaque, sealed envelopes. The study protocol was approved by the Institutional Ethics Committee, and all participants provided written informed consent.

2.2 Interventions

All participants received standardized lectures covering osteology of the skull, including cranial and facial bones, foramina, fossae, and the cranial base. Following the lecture, participants engaged in self-directed learning sessions twice per week for two weeks (total four sessions, 60 minutes each). 

The intervention group (*n* = 48) studied polylactic acid (PLA) 3D-printed full-scale skull models derived from high-resolution CT scans of an adult male cadaver. The models retained natural coloration in a single hue (ivory white) to emphasize structural morphology without the distraction of painted sutures. Students were permitted to handle, rotate, disassemble (calvaria separated from the base), and physically inspect internal and external cranial features. 

The control group (*n* = 48) utilized the university’s standard learning resources, including textbook atlases, anatomical charts, and high-resolution digital 2D images displayed on tablets. These students did not have access to 3D-printed models, plastic skull models, or cadaveric specimens during the intervention period.

2.3 Outcome Measures

Primary outcomes were the change from baseline to post-intervention in (i) theoretical knowledge assessed via a 50-item multiple-choice question (MCQ) examination (score range 0–100) and (ii) practical anatomical identification using a 25-station objective structured practical examination (OSPE) focused on skull osteology (score range 0–50). 

Secondary outcomes included spatial visualization ability measured by the Purdue Spatial Visualization Test–Rotations (PSVT-R; score range 0–30) and student satisfaction evaluated using a 10-item validated questionnaire employing a 5-point Likert scale (1 = strongly disagree to 5 = strongly agree), yielding a maximum composite score of 50. All assessments were administered at baseline (pre-intervention) and within 48 hours following the final learning session (post-intervention). Assessors grading OSPE stations and scoring questionnaires were blinded to group allocation.

2.4 Statistical Analysis

Sample size was calculated *a priori* based on an expected 10-point difference in post-intervention theoretical scores (effect size *d* = 0.65), assuming a two-tailed alpha of 0.05 and 80% power, yielding a minimum of 38 participants per group; we enrolled 48 per group to account for 20% attrition. Data were analyzed using SPSS version 26.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD) and compared using independent samples *t*-tests or Mann-Whitney *U* tests depending on distribution normality. Categorical variables were analyzed using chi-square tests. Paired *t*-tests evaluated within-group pre-post changes. Analysis of covariance (ANCOVA) was performed for post-intervention scores, adjusting for baseline values. Statistical significance was set at *p* < 0.05.

3. Results and Analysis

Of 112 students screened, 96 met eligibility criteria and were randomized (48 per group). All randomized participants completed the study, resulting in no attrition. The two groups were comparable at baseline regarding age, sex distribution, prior academic performance, and pre-intervention scores for theoretical knowledge (*p* = 0.78), OSPE (*p* = 0.82), and PSVT-R (*p* = 0.61) (Table 1).

Post-intervention, the 3D-printed model group achieved significantly higher mean theoretical examination scores compared with the control group (86.4 ± 7.2 vs. 79.8 ± 8.5; mean difference 6.6; 95% CI 3.1 to 10.1; *p* < 0.001 after adjusting for baseline scores). Within-group improvements were also more pronounced in the intervention cohort (mean increase 14.2 ± 6.8 points) than in controls (mean increase 9.8 ± 7.4 points; *p* = 0.002 for between-group difference in gain scores).

In the practical OSPE, the 3D-printed model group demonstrated superior identification accuracy (42.1 ± 4.3 out of 50, 84.2%) relative to the control group (36.5 ± 5.8, 73.0%; *p* < 0.001). Notably, the largest disparities were observed in structures requiring complex spatial localization, such as the greater wing of the sphenoid, foramen lacerum, and internal acoustic meatus.

Spatial visualization ability, as measured by the PSVT-R, improved significantly in the intervention group (post-test 24.1 ± 3.2 vs. pre-test 18.7 ± 3.5; Δ = 5.4 ± 3.1) compared with modest gains in the control group (post-test 21.2 ± 3.4 vs. pre-test 19.1 ± 3.2; Δ = 2.1 ± 2.8; *p* < 0.001 for between-group comparison).

Student satisfaction scores were substantially higher among participants utilizing 3D-printed models (composite score 46.2 ± 3.8 vs. 37.1 ± 5.2; *p* < 0.001). Specifically, intervention-group students reported significantly greater agreement with statements regarding tactile learning utility (4.8 ± 0.4), ease of understanding 3D relationships (4.7 ± 0.5), and overall educational value (4.6 ± 0.5). No adverse events or logistical issues were reported during the trial.

4. Discussion

This randomized controlled trial provides robust evidence that 3D-printed skull models confer significant educational advantages over conventional 2D instructional resources in undergraduate anatomy education. Participants utilizing tactile, manipulable models demonstrated superior theoretical knowledge, enhanced practical identification skills, and markedly improved spatial visualization compared with their peers relying on textbooks and digital images. These findings align with cognitive load theory and embodied cognition frameworks, which posit that multisensory engagement—particularly haptic exploration—reduces extraneous cognitive load and facilitates the construction of accurate mental spatial representations.

The magnitude of benefit was especially pronounced for anatomically complex regions, such as the cranial base and sphenoid bone, where 2D representations are inherently limited in conveying depth and orientation. Our results corroborate and extend prior non-randomized studies suggesting that 3D models improve comprehension of intricate cranial topography. Importantly, the significant improvement in PSVT-R scores within the intervention group suggests that 3D-printed models may cultivate transferable spatial reasoning skills, which are critical not only for anatomy but also for future surgical training and radiological interpretation.

Student satisfaction data further underscore the pedagogical acceptability of 3D-printed models. The high satisfaction ratings likely reflect increased learner autonomy and engagement afforded by physical manipulation, contrasting with the passive viewing required by atlases and screens. From a curricular standpoint, these models may serve as a cost-effective, ethically uncomplicated bridge in programs where cadaver availability is restricted. However, we acknowledge limitations. The single-center design and brief intervention period preclude generalizations regarding long-term knowledge retention. Additionally, we utilized monochromatic models; future investigations should examine whether color-coded models highlighting muscle origins, vascular channels, or nervous pathways yield incremental benefits. Finally, the absence of a cadaveric dissection arm limits direct comparisons with the traditional gold standard.

5. Conclusion

Integration of 3D-printed skull models into undergraduate anatomy instruction significantly improves medical students’ theoretical knowledge, practical osteological identification, spatial visualization ability, and learning satisfaction compared with conventional 2D educational resources. These findings support the structured implementation of 3D printing technology as an evidence-based adjunct in modern anatomy curricula, particularly for teaching complex cranial anatomy. Future research should explore long-term retention outcomes, cost-effectiveness analyses, and the incremental value of multi-material and color-coded 3D-printed models.

title: Can cropland management practices lower net greenhouse emissions without compromising yield?
text:
Can cropland management practices lower net greenhouse emissions without compromising yield?

---

Abstract

Agriculture contributes approximately 10–12 % of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, yet cropland soils also offer significant potential for climate mitigation. This study evaluates whether alternative management can reduce net GHG emissions without sacrificing crop yield. A three-year field experiment (2021–2023) in Iowa, USA compared four treatments in a maize–soybean rotation: conventional tillage (CT), no-till with cover crops (NT), reduced tillage with optimized nitrogen (RT), and an integrated system (IM) combining no-till, cover crops, optimized N, and compost amendment. We measured soil N₂O and CH₄ fluxes, soil organic carbon (SOC) changes, and grain yield. Yields did not differ significantly across treatments (*p* = 0.31). However, N₂O emissions were 48 % lower under IM compared to CT (1.8 vs. 3.5 kg N₂O–N ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹; *p* < 0.01). The IM system achieved a net negative GHG balance (−0.95 Mg CO₂-eq ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹) due to enhanced SOC sequestration (+1.80 Mg CO₂-eq ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹), whereas CT was a net emitter (+1.95 Mg CO₂-eq ha⁻¹ yr⁻¹). We conclude that integrated cropland management can substantially lower net GHG emissions while maintaining productivity, offering a viable pathway for climate-smart agriculture.

Keywords: Greenhouse gas mitigation; Climate-smart agriculture; Soil carbon sequestration; No-tillage; Cover crops; Net global warming potential

---

Introduction

Agriculture is both a contributor to and a potential victim of climate change, responsible for roughly 10–12 % of global anthropogenic greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions.
